- The Eve looped-replay fix is now proven at scenario grade: the automated Eve player-loop scenario - which was deliberately left requiring the OLD broken behavior as a tripwire - failed exactly as designed on the fixed build (only the three obsolete failure signatures missing, everything else green), and was re-pinned to require the healthy state instead: the replayed transfer re-aims, keeps its true tilted arc, and arrives inside Eve's sphere of influence at the recorded handoff instant. The tracking-station scenario now sees a genuinely re-aimed chain, and the deliberate-faithful comparison scenario measured byte-identical before/after - proof the fix touches only what it claims to. Scenario-spec and docs only in this change; the behavior itself shipped in the two preceding entries.
- Fixed a wrong arrival instant in re-planned interplanetary replays, found by the new automated Eve checks on their very first run. When a replay re-plans its transfer, it asks the game's own trajectory solver where the route enters the destination's gravitational sphere, and that answer is what the replay hands over to the arrival leg on. But the route starts at the launch planet's centre - already deep inside the launch planet's own sphere - so the solver frequently answered with the moment the route LEAVES the launch planet instead: the departure instant, at which the route is billions of metres from the destination. It was accepted without question. The re-plan now checks that answer - the moment must be after departure, and the route must actually be inside the destination's sphere at it - and where it fails, falls back to the direct arrival search the code already had, which finds the real moment from the same route. Nothing that used to be accepted is now rejected: a route whose reported moment fails the check is still flown, just with the correct arrival instant. Routes to Duna were measured unaffected before and after. This was not caused by the tilted-destination fix below - most of the affected routes were ones that fix never touches - but that fix is what made these routes get as far as the solver, and without this correction they would have arrived at the right place at the wrong time.
- Fixed the Eve replay defect diagnosed the same day: a looped mission to a tilted destination no longer quietly degrades into a verbatim replay that flies to where the destination used to be. When a replay re-plans its transfer for the current launch window, it checks whether the route's plane can be tidied onto the destination's own plane; for a tilted destination like Eve that tidy-up is impossible from where the ship departs, and the code used to answer that by throwing the whole route away - falling back to replaying the recorded transfer one launch-window cycle late, which missed Eve by four and a half times the width of its gravitational sphere. It now keeps the route it already has: that steeper arc genuinely passes through Eve, and whether the replay arrives is decided where it always was, by the arrival check at the end of the re-plan. Nothing about the check itself changed, every other reason for rejecting a route still rejects it, and a route that would travel the wrong way round is still refused. **This changes what you see, and it is meant to.** On a tilted destination the replayed transfer arc can look visibly steeper - tipped out of the flat plane the planets mostly share - than the route you actually flew, because you reached Eve by changing plane halfway there and a single arc cannot imitate that. The steep arc is the one that arrives; the flat-looking alternative was a ghost missing the planet by four planet-spheres. The arc's tilt also differs from one launch window to the next, because it depends on where the destination sits relative to its own tilt at that date. Destinations that sit close to the flat plane, such as Duna, are untouched - their tidy-up always succeeds and behaves exactly as before. Also added: when a replayed transfer does still fall back to the recorded one for a launch window, the log now says so with a warning naming the mission member, the window and the reason, instead of leaving it to be inferred from a line that isn't there.
- Settled the diagnosis behind the Eve replay defect measured the same day - the one where a looped Eve mission is accepted for re-aiming and then quietly replays the recorded transfer instead, flying to where Eve used to be - and pinned its arithmetic as headless tests, so the fix can be judged against numbers instead of a log reading. Three findings, each now a test. The safety check that refuses to re-aim this window is fed only the departure point and the destination's orbital plane, neither of which changes with the route being tried, so all twenty-seven candidate routes are refused identically and no amount of searching can rescue the window. The steep transfer plane it objects to is the only plane a single arc through both ends can have, and the flatter plane it would prefer misses Eve by three and a half times the width of its gravitational sphere - so the check's verdict is correct, and what is wrong is what the code then does with that verdict: throw away a route that was already sane, going the right way, and passing through Eve. And the recorded flight itself reached Eve by changing plane halfway there, which a single arc can never imitate - which rules out the two cheapest-looking fixes. Test-only; no gameplay change.
- A third Eve scenario completes the side-by-side comparison the replay program has wanted since the force-faithful toggle shipped: the same recorded Eve mission, replayed with re-aiming deliberately switched off. It measured two things nobody had numbers for. First, a forced-faithful loop schedules itself differently from a re-aimed one - it overlays up to twenty staggered copies of the replay (the re-aimed form runs one at a time), and the "warp to next launch" button rides that stagger. Second, and the reason it was built: the destination-approach diagnostic fires on a deliberately-faithful interplanetary replay exactly as designed - five detections per run, at the arrival of each staggered copy plus one at the recorded Mun flyby (the Mun isn't there anymore at the shifted date either, which nobody had thought about) - and the measured miss distances of these BENIGN detections bracket the miss distance of the genuine defect the diagnostic caught earlier the same day. That settles a standing question: the diagnostic can never be promoted to a hard failure on miss distance alone, and the record now says so with the numbers. Scenario-spec and docs only; no gameplay change.
- A second Eve scenario makes the first automated tracking-station observation of a looped inward-transfer arrival: it arms the recorded Eve mission's loop, warps past the replay's arrival into Eve's sphere of influence, saves, and re-boots into the tracking station - where the replay really does materialize, Eve-framed, on its own orbit line. Building it surfaced two things worth their own records: a third sighting of the known scene-reload race (a recorder re-arms itself in the window a run just cleared, roughly one attempt in four across three different scenarios now - absorbed by the standard retry), and a genuine new finding - a save written from the tracking station scene silently loses the outcome classification on debris recordings, something a player quitting from the tracking station would hit too; filed with byte-level evidence rather than fixed in passing. Scenario-spec and docs only; no gameplay change.
- A new automated scenario replays the recorded Eve mission the way a player would - load the save, arm the mission's loop, warp to the next launch window, then follow the replay across the Mun flyby, the escape into interplanetary space, and the arrival at Eve - and its first flights produced the program's biggest single haul of measurements to date. The headline: the destination-approach diagnostic shipped earlier (the one that checks whether a replayed transfer's drawn arc actually reaches its destination's sphere of influence, and had never once fired) produced its first genuine detection, five flights out of five: on this mission the replay engine accepts the loop for re-aiming but then quietly gives up on the transfer re-plan - Eve's tilted orbit fails a safety check for every candidate route it tries - so it silently replays the recorded transfer verbatim instead, one launch-window cycle late, and that replayed transfer misses Eve by four and a half times the width of its gravitational sphere. A player watching that loop would see their ship fly to where Eve used to be. The finding is filed with exact numbers against the long-open "looped transfer never arrives" investigation rather than patched here. The same flights also bought: the first-ever measurement of the loop scheduler compressing a parking-orbit wait out of a replay (eleven million game-seconds cut - a coverage cell previously recorded as unreachable by any committed test), the first loop unit whose recording is longer than its own launch-window cycle (the scheduler correctly doubles the replay cadence rather than mis-aligning), and two failed runs that exposed a blind spot in the map-flicker detector - it cannot tell a genuine line flicker from two legitimate display transitions squeezed together by back-to-back time jumps, something only the test harness's instantaneous clock can produce - filed with both artifacts, and the scenario re-paced to jump like a player rather than the detector being loosened. Scenario-spec, fixtures and docs only; no gameplay change.
- A new committed test fixture holds a real recorded Eve mission - a complete flight that launches, waits out the transfer window in low Kerbin orbit, crosses to Eve on the program's first inward interplanetary transfer, captures and parks at 5,000 km, and saves the recording there - so the looped-replay validation work can replay a genuine inward-transfer flight instead of re-flying the half-hour mission every time. Producing it re-flew the Eve orbit mission green on the first attempt (its second green flight) and replaced that scenario's provisional recording-count and wall-time numbers with measured ones. Measuring the fixture also established a fact the follow-up lanes are built around: the recorded mission is 7% longer than the Kerbin-Eve launch-window cycle, a regime the replay scheduler treats specially, so those lanes measure what the scheduler actually does with it rather than assume the shape the Duna and moon lanes see. Test assets and scenario-spec only; no gameplay change.
- Four new automated scenarios now replay the two committed moon missions the way a player would - Mun and Minmus, each watched both from the flight scene and from the tracking station - and they cover the other kind of looped mission entirely: a flight to a moon of the planet it launched from never needs its transfer re-aimed at a moving target, so these lanes check the replay takes the faithful road and fail if any of the re-aim machinery reports for duty. Three of the four fly green unattended in under a minute each and are armed as hard checks that a pure replay-watching session writes nothing permanent into the save; among other things they confirm that a mission looped through two and three cycles still arrives at the same place each time (no drift detectable at the sampling resolution), that the tracking station really does materialize a looped moon arrival on its own orbit line, and they produced the suite's first successful entry into ghost watch mode - which in turn pinned down how close you actually have to be, every previous write-up having assumed a far more generous distance (see the bullet below for what that correction does and does not settle). The fourth stands deliberately RED on a real finding rather than being quietly excused: after one large time jump that lands inside a Minmus capture, the replay's map icon sits 131 degrees behind its own (otherwise correct) orbit line, identically on both flights, and that is recorded for whoever fixes it rather than budgeted away. Scenario-spec and docs only; no gameplay change.
- Two new committed test fixtures hold a real recorded Mun mission and a real recorded Minmus mission - each a complete flight that launches, transfers, captures, parks in the moon's own sphere of influence and saves the recording there - so the looped-replay validation work can replay genuine moon flights instead of re-flying the missions every time. Producing them also caught and fixed a stale automated check on the Mun lane that had been copied from a different mission's flight log and was never actually true of the Mun flight profile - and rather than just dropping it, the Mun lane now checks the opposite: the leftover stage that check expected in Kerbin orbit has never once appeared there across the three measured Mun flights, so the lane fails if one ever does. Test assets and scenario-spec only; no gameplay change.
- Two new automated scenarios now fly the whole player-side replay loop unattended, and both are armed as hard checks: one drives the sequence a person actually performs after a mission is recorded (load the save, arm the mission's loop, warp to the next launch window, press Watch, follow the replay forward across the arrival, press Watch again at the parked tail), and one is the first automated observation of a looped interplanetary replay from the tracking station - which answered positively: the re-aimed member does materialize there at its arrival epoch, on its own orbit line, with the debris member correctly skipped. Both measured things nobody had numbers for before: ghost watch mode is camera-only and refuses far-away ghosts, so a parked observer at the replay's arrival tail (644 km away on a shared 1,038 km-radius orbit) was refused a watch rather than being categorically unable to watch it, and the tracking-station observation window this shape can buy is about a second. (Two things about that refusal were written down wrongly and are now corrected. First, the write-ups reasoned that anything closer than 300 km is watchable; the moon scenarios in the bullet above disproved that by refusing a watch at 144, 191 and 199 km and succeeding at 51.5 km, which places the real boundary somewhere between 51.5 and 144 km. Second - and this is the correction to the correction - those write-ups then blamed the ghost-visibility range for the refusal, which is not what the code does: the distance test on the path a player's Watch press takes really is the 300 km one (305 km to leave), so it is not what turned the player away, and what did turn them away is not yet known. The measurements and every conclusion drawn from them are unchanged; only the explanation was wrong, and the open question now has a named, cheap experiment attached to it. The product's own on-screen text and button tooltip say 300 km, which is a true statement about the distance test - the follow-up filed here is not to change that number but to work out why a player is refused far inside the range the game quotes them, and then tell them.) Scenario-spec and docs only; no gameplay change.
- New Settings > Looping toggle, "Force faithful loop playback (no re-aim)": a looped interplanetary mission normally re-aims each transfer at the destination's actual position for that launch window, so the ghost still arrives; turning this on replays the recorded trajectory verbatim on the loop clock instead. Off by default, so nothing changes unless you enable it - it exists for comparing the two side by side and for players who prefer to watch exactly what they flew, accepting that the verbatim transfer will miss the destination on most cycles. Affects only looped inter-body missions. (Superseded later in this same release: the settings simplification - see Settings, "The Settings window got a lot smaller" - removed this toggle from the window. Re-aiming is what ships; the verbatim mode survives only as a field the automated-testing harness sets for its A/B lanes.)
- Continued the looped-interplanetary arrival-validation program onto the flight scene (the surface the known re-aim arrival defect actually lives on, which the earlier map-view lane never drives): a new always-cheap seam-teleport detector on ghost playback (raises a gated diagnostic line when a looped ghost's position jumps by more than 1,000 km at a trajectory-segment boundary - healthy recorded seams measure under 10 km; only active when ghost render tracing is enabled), a fix for map/tracking-station diagnostic lines attributing a ghost to a stale recording after the driving recording changes, and two new automated flight-scene scenarios that replay the recorded Duna mission through both sphere-of-influence handoffs in faithful and re-aimed modes side by side. Test-tooling and read-only observability; no gameplay change. A third flight-scene scenario (the companion: the recorded mission re-flown live alongside its own engaged loop replay) went through a tuning pass: its course-correction budget widened past the measured cycle-2 cost (closing the Duna encounter the first reading runs missed), its post-park seam dwell REMOVED after review established the ghost-visibility range (120 km) makes any parked observation of the arrival handoff impossible, a refused-backward-time-jump guard token added (the seam rejects backward jumps; the earlier run passed only because post-mission steps don't gate), and the remaining co-location design work recorded; scenario-spec and docs only.
- New developer diagnostic that notices when a looped mission's replayed transfer arc stops short of its destination instead of arriving: at each recorded sphere-of-influence handoff it checks whether the arc actually being drawn reaches the destination planet's sphere of influence at the moment the flight got there, and reports it once if the arc dead-ends outside it. It fills a real blind spot - the existing render checks each measure one leg against its own reference, so none of them can see the gap between two legs, and the main one deliberately stands down on exactly the re-aimed replays where this shows up. Off unless map render tracing is enabled, read-only, and it reports rather than fails a run; no gameplay change. It also reports on itself: once per pass it logs how many destination-approach checks it actually performed and, for each one it did not, why - so a silent run can be told apart from an unwatched one by reading the log, instead of reconstructing the answer from the recordings afterwards. That self-report immediately earned its keep. When the check first flew, the five looped-replay scenarios it flew on were all read as never having exercised it - the conclusion being that each parks its clock on the last leg of the recording, leaving no next handoff to measure - and that reading was reconstructed by hand from the recordings because the check could not yet speak for itself. Flying the five again with the self-report switched on showed the hand reconstruction was wrong on two of them: the interplanetary workflow scenario and the flight-scene Minmus one each do reach a real handoff, and on both the drawn arc arrives INSIDE the destination's sphere - the first genuine reading this check has produced, and a healthy one, on the very shape of arrival the known defect lives in. The other three sit past their handoff and genuinely have nothing to measure, exactly as reconstructed. Both readings reproduced on three consecutive runs each, so the two scenarios that reach a handoff now REQUIRE that they did, which is the difference between a check that ran and a check that looked at something. A pre-merge review then found one case where the check would have been confidently wrong, and it is now refused rather than reported: when a replay's transfer is re-aimed AND its arrival is re-timed - which happens on the departure shape that leaves from a parking orbit, where the transfer is re-planned around a faster route and so gets there days earlier than the recording did - the check was still sampling the drawn arc at the moment the ORIGINAL flight arrived, when the arc was nowhere near the destination yet. That is a wrong measurement on a correct arc, and it would have looked exactly like the fault the check exists to find. It now detects the re-timing (by comparing the replay's own arc end against the recorded handoff) and reports that it could not measure, instead of reporting a fault. The refusal is narrow by design and both scenarios that buy a real reading were re-flown to prove it: neither lost its measurement. Also renamed the "could not measure" bucket to say what it actually covers - a broken drawn conic lands there too, not only the Sun-as-destination case its old name described.

- Five automated looped-replay scenarios had been running an armed rendering-fault sweep without ever checking that the thing doing the looking had looked at anything - a green run and a run where the replay never appeared were indistinguishable. Each now requires a line the render probe emits only once it has actually resolved a replaying craft, and forbids that line reporting any position drift; all five re-flown to prove it. Chasing that turned up two things worth writing down. The check people reached for first (a probe summary reporting a non-zero craft count) turns out to be a stopwatch race rather than a real signal - the summary is rate-limited to one line every five seconds on a shared timer, the first one fires a couple of milliseconds after tracing switches on with nothing loaded yet, and four of the five scenarios finish inside that window, in two and a half to four seconds; the fifth ran a shade over five seconds and its second summary line landed fourteen milliseconds past the five-second mark, promptly buying the line the other four could not, which is exactly why it is the wrong thing to require. The second is a real gap in a render check: the parity check that compares a replayed orbit against the recorded one stands down whenever a recorded arc happens to be stored in several consecutive pieces - which is the normal shape of an arrival - because it compares the pieces' internal time-references and finds them different even though the arc is identical. It affects a measurement, not what is drawn, and is filed with a measured diagnosis and two fix directions rather than papered over. Scenario-spec and docs only; no gameplay change.

- Corrected the automated-testing record for one moon scenario and filed the flake it was hiding: its three most recent runs had been written up as three identical failures on the scenario's own known finding, but one of them never got that far - it was thrown out as an invalid run when a mid-run scene reload was refused because a recorder had re-armed itself in the window the run had just cleared. That is a second sighting of a race first measured a day earlier on a different scenario, whose fix was described at the time as making the outcome deterministic; this run had that fix and lost anyway, so the fix narrows the window rather than closing it, and the race is now filed in its own right with both sightings' timings. Docs only; no gameplay change.

- Recorded a coverage fact rather than leaving it as open backlog: one automated-testing dimension - compressing a long parking loiter out of a replayed mission - cannot be covered by any test fixture that exists, and it is not for want of writing a scenario. Missions to a moon of their own launch planet never take the code path that produces loiter cuts at all, and the one interplanetary fixture deliberately jumps its launch to the transfer window rather than waiting in orbit, so its parking phase is three-quarters of a single lap - nothing whole to cut. What would actually cover it is now written down precisely, including the honest wall-clock cost of the obvious option (a scenario that waits for the window instead of jumping to it would sit through roughly two hundred in-game days of fast-forward) and the two missing pieces of machinery the other option needs. Docs only; no gameplay change.

- The automated-testing harness can now drive the exact sequence a player performs to watch a looped mission replay, which until now only a human at the keyboard could do: two new automation commands, one that fast-forwards the clock to a looped mission's next launch window through the very same code path the Missions window's "Warp to..." button uses (including its 15-second pre-launch lead, so the run arrives on the pad just before lift-off instead of a quarter of a minute after it), and one that enters ghost watch mode on a replaying flight - choosing the watchable ghost exactly the way the window's "Watch" button chooses it, and confirming the camera actually took hold before reporting success, because the underlying call fails silently and would otherwise report a watch that never happened. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.

- Started the looped-interplanetary arrival-validation lane (the missing playback half beside the existing re-aim solver gates): a new synthetic test corpus carrying the real flown Duna-transfer geometry, and a new automated scenario that checks - across both recorded sphere-of-influence handoffs and at arrival - that recorded-segment playback resolves positions continuously and lands inside Duna's sphere of influence, the exact property the known looped re-aim rendering defect violates. Includes a small pure position helper that propagates reference bodies to the queried time (the stock shortcut anchors at the body's current position, which silently breaks any comparison across two planets' frames). The lane's second half adds a new automation command that switches a saved mission's loop playback on or off through the same code path the Missions window uses, and a new automated scenario that loads the recorded Duna flight, arms its loop, and watches the replay on the map across both sphere-of-influence handoffs and the arrival - the first unattended observation of a looped interplanetary replay. Flown the same day: re-aim engaged for the direct member, the replay crossed both handoffs with a clean anomaly sweep at map scale, and the hand-off into the Duna frame at arrival is now a hard-required check - the known re-aim arrival defect did not reproduce on the map surface (its measuring instrument lives on the flight-scene path), so the scenario stands as the armed regression floor for the deferred fix rather than its reproduction. A five-agent post-review hardening pass then added a launch-phase-vs-ideal drift assertion to the pad-aligned mission machine (the in-flight window guard structurally cannot see an ephemeris miss - the ASAP planner always burns within one park orbit), widened the craft drift gate over every committed copy of the DD1 craft (the nightly boots a fixture copy, not the forge base), made the fixture harvester refuse to overwrite a recorded-state fixture without its keep flag, and pinned the recorded fixture's recording ids and schema generation against the C# loader constant so a generation bump cannot silently degrade the fixture into one that tests nothing. Test-tooling plus one read-only helper; no gameplay change.

- Added the automated duna-direct lane, the fixture producer for the long-deferred looped interplanetary re-aim fix: a new probe-only craft authored deterministically from stock parts (with a byte-level drift gate), and a new automated mission that time-jumps ON THE PAD to the Kerbin-Duna ejection window - so the recorded flight contains no parking-orbit wait at all - then ascends, ejects directly, corrects mid-course, captures into a low Duna orbit deliberately below Ike's path, and commits the recording in-flight. A moon encounter anywhere in the flight (Ike at arrival, Mun or Minmus on the way out) fails the run by name instead of quietly passing, because the clean recording is the entire point. The launch-window math is pure, headlessly unit-tested Kepler arithmetic over the stock planetary constants. Flown green the same day: the recorded flight measured a 54-day pad time-jump and an ejection planned 30 minutes after liftoff, captured into a low Duna orbit with the moon-avoidance checks silent, and the produced save is committed as a reusable fixture so follow-up validation work replays the recording instead of re-flying the mission. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.

- The Recordings window is now called Missions: the main-window button and the window title both read "Missions", and the Missions tab is the first and default tab, with the raw Recordings table as the second tab.
- New Settings > Interface toggle with Basic and Advanced modes: Basic shows only Timeline, Missions, Logistics and Settings and hides the power-user windows and sections, while Advanced is the full UI unchanged. Existing installs stay on Advanced; fresh installs start on Basic, and switching modes only changes what is shown, never what is recorded or played back.
- The Timeline's GoTo buttons now open the mission a flight belongs to instead of the raw recordings table, so they work in both Basic and Advanced. The Missions window opens on the Missions tab and scrolls to that mission, un-hiding it first if the Archive filter was covering it. The button is greyed out on the few rows that belong to no mission, such as manual Gloops recordings.
- In Basic mode, nearby-craft alerts drop the instruction to open Real Spawn Control, whose button that mode hides, and keep the useful part: which craft is nearby and when it departs.
- Supply-route pause and resume actions are now recorded on the career timeline, so rewinding past them restores the route's pause history consistently with everything else; Send Once runs are marked as one-shot cycles in the timeline, and the "Sending one cycle" state now survives save and reload.
- Supply routes now respect the timeline across a rewind: a route created after the rewind point disappears from the Logistics window and stops dispatching (previously it kept running before its own creation), goes dormant instead of being lost, and automatically reappears (paused, ready to re-activate) once the re-flown timeline passes its original creation point, as long as its source recordings still exist. Routes created before the rewind point now also resume their delivery schedule correctly on the re-flown timeline instead of silently skipping cycles.
- Dormant routes are no longer invisible: the Logistics window shows a collapsed "Dormant Routes" section listing each one with the date it will reappear and a Delete button, and a route that auto-pauses or recovers because its source recordings vanished or changed during play now records that pause and resume on the career timeline.

- Supply routes no longer lose cargo when the destination is full: a route now waits ("Held: no room for X" / "Held: no slot for 'part'") until the destination has room for the full delivery, instead of charging the origin and silently dropping whatever did not fit. If room disappears mid-cycle, the route's detail panel now reports exactly what was lost.
- A supply route held on a missing stored part now names the part instead of showing an internal code, and says when the part is actually there but its charge, fuel, or contents no longer match the recorded cargo.
- Added a developer-only automated visual-validation scenario, the first of its kind: after flying and committing the automated Mun-orbit mission, the harness rewinds so the just-flown mission replays as ghosts, points the map camera at it, and watches the whole replay - at 1x, through a time-warp ramp, and across the recorded Mun boundary crossing - while Parsek's own render-parity instrumentation measures every frame. The scenario fails if the watched replay turns out to be empty (the exact false-green an earlier scenario once passed on), and it records how often the map-render anomaly detectors fire on a real flight so those detectors can later be armed as hard checks with evidence-based budgets. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-testing harness can now assert that a flight actually RECORDED something, not just that a recording file exists. Until now a scenario could only pin how many recordings a run produced, and two empty recordings are still two files - so even an exact count could not tell a recorded flight from one that captured nothing, which is the blind spot an orbital-EVA recording bug sat in. Scenarios can now declare windows on the recorded trajectory-point counts, read out of the produced save itself, including a limit on how many recordings may come back empty - so one healthy recording can no longer hide empty ones beside it. Every run reports those counts whether or not it declares a window, so a window can be sized from a real flight before it is switched on. Landed report-only: it reports on the orbital-EVA scenario today and moves no run's verdict until an operator arms it against a measured flight. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer map-render diagnostics no longer report a false problem when a replaying ghost's map trajectory passes between its two drawing surfaces. While the drawn flight path covers a launch or burn, the ghost's predicted-orbit line is deliberately hidden so the two do not overlap - and it stays hidden in the stretches between recorded flight-path segments, where the orbit being predicted swings wildly from one frame to the next and drawing it would look far worse than leaving it out. Under a fast time-warp ramp a whole recorded burn replays in a handful of frames, and the detector that watches for a flickering orbit line saw only that line going off and back on, so it called it a flicker. It now asks whether the ghost's flight path was actually being drawn on every frame the orbit line was hidden, and stays quiet when it was - while still reporting the case that matters, where the line goes dark and nothing at all is drawn in its place. Diagnostics-only, off by default; nothing about how the map looks in game changed.
- The automated-testing harness now fails a run whose KSP.log shows more raw Unity exceptions than that scenario has ever produced when healthy. The scan itself existed but was report-only everywhere; it is now an armed gate on 14 scenarios, each with a ceiling taken from that scenario's own measured history (zero for the eleven scenarios that have never produced one; small measured ceilings for the three with a known benign source, including the tracking-station scenario whose ceiling comes from the arithmetic of a diagnosed stock shutdown race rather than from the highest count seen). The gate was proven in both directions before arming: every armed scenario re-flew green at its final ceiling, and a deliberately impossible ceiling on one scenario turned the run red exactly as designed before being reverted. Noisy long-flight scenarios stay report-only with the reason recorded per scenario. The harness's dry-run plan now also says per scenario whether this check can fail the run, instead of a hard-coded "report-only" label that had just become wrong for all 14. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Seven of the map-render anomaly detectors that previously only reported are now hard checks: a raise of any of them fails the scenarios that fly with render tracing on. The promotion was made on measured silence rather than hope - five full map-dwell replays (about 130 ghost-sampled frames each), fresh runs of every tracer-armed scenario, and 155 historical tracer-on runs never raised any of the seven. The two detectors that are measuring instruments rather than defect signals (a drawing-coverage probe and a shadow-comparison probe) deliberately stay report-only, with the reasoning written down next to the code. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-testing harness now leaves something a human can look at after every run, green runs included: each run's KSP.log (bounded, with an explicit truncation marker on oversize logs) and any screenshots taken during the run's window are copied into the harness results folder, and a self-contained per-run contact-sheet HTML page shows the captured images next to the run's key log lines - the in-game batch tally, every render-parity summary, and every anomaly raise with the surrounding per-frame probe readings - alongside the verifier verdicts, plus a newest-first index page listing all runs with color-coded verdicts. Purely additive and verdict-neutral: artifact or page trouble only warns, it can never change a run's result, the run's verdict is written durably before any artifact copying starts, and the existing heavy non-PASS log collection is unchanged. A retention pass bounds the growth: only the newest per-run artifact folders are kept (40 folders / 2 GiB), while the lightweight contact pages - which embed the extracted log lines as text - are kept for every run. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-testing harness can now run Parsek's rewind and re-fly self-tests unattended. Parsek ships 37 in-game tests for that area - more than for any other single area, and the largest set nothing automated had ever run - because most of them only mean anything inside a live re-fly and nothing could set one up on its own. Two passes now run automatically: one covering the tests that apply when no re-fly is in progress, and one at the Space Centre for the tests that only apply there. Two passes rather than one because the tests contradict each other by design - twelve require a re-fly to be in progress, and four were written to require that none is (five now, since one of the fixes below adds the same guard to another) - so no single pass could ever run them all. Running them turned up faults in the tests themselves that no earlier run could have seen; four are fixed here across three tests: two of those tests assumed nothing else was going on in the save and quietly broke when something was (one of them in two separate ways), and the third consumed the re-fly it was handed without giving it back, which silently stopped nine later tests from running at all. Four more failing tests are recorded for a future pass rather than fixed here. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The Space-Centre pass of the rewind self-tests now runs fully green and covers one more test than before. Its first run had two honest gaps: one self-test made Parsek log an internal error while still passing (its synthetic test setup omitted the rewind-point record every real rewind carries; the setup is now shaped like the real thing, and fixing that surfaced - and fixed - a second setup mistake that hid the launch row the test checks), and one self-test could never run because the test-data generator had no way to mark an injected flight as unfinished (it can now, and the previously-unrunnable check runs and passes). The four existing scenarios that share those test fixtures were re-flown green the same day to confirm nothing they gate on moved. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Two more in-game test areas now run unattended as well: the stock-API assumptions Parsek's math depends on (clock monotonicity, part-lookup identity, floating-origin drift) and the save-format round-trip checks, including the decimal-comma one that only ever misbehaves on machines set to certain languages. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added a measuring instrument for a known coordinate-frame discrepancy in the code that predicts where a falling vessel ends up after you leave the scene. The discrepancy has been documented for months but deliberately left alone, because the correction turns on how two coordinate systems map onto each other - something that has to be measured in the running game rather than worked out on paper, and nobody had a cheap way to measure it. Two new self-tests now take that reading automatically on any flight-scene test run: one asks the prediction code where the vessel currently is and compares its answer against where the game says the vessel actually is, and the other checks whether a predicted tail's recorded orientation survives the round trip back out through the replay code. Both print the exact numbers, in the failure text and in the log, and both were expected to fail until the correction landed - that failure WAS the reading, and it is the reading the correction below was built on. Now that the correction has landed they both pass, and they stay in place as regression guards: if either ever moves off zero again, the frames have drifted apart once more and the exact numbers are back in the log without anyone having to build an instrument first. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Six more in-game test areas now run unattended, chosen by reading every test's actual preconditions rather than by category name: the log-format contracts (run on a career save so the career-money sanity checks really execute instead of quietly checking nothing on a sandbox one), the diagnostics report, the ghost map-presence bookkeeping and ghost-audio lifecycle (both run over the full injected recording corpus so the checks that quietly do nothing over an empty world get real ghosts to check), localized vessel-name resolution, and the crew reservation and seat-matching system - the last on the one save in the fixture library that actually has both a free seat and spare crew, without which most of its checks would silently sit out. Reading first also caught, before any flight was wasted on it, that the automated game installations had their per-ship audio pinned to zero, which made "did the ghost's engine sound actually start" impossible to test on them - overall silence is kept by the master volume alone now. Three crew self-tests also stopped leaving a stray crew-status event behind in the save after they run. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Parsek's mod-compatibility self-tests finally run somewhere real: the automated-testing harness gained a second, fully modded game installation (Waterfall with its effect packs, ReStock and ReStock+, Kopernicus, B9PartSwitch and friends - the same set as the development install), provisioned and verified by the same machinery as the stock one, and two new nightly scenarios run the 17 Waterfall- and ReStock-compatibility self-tests on it. Those tests have always skipped themselves on a stock install - on the modded one, 15 of the 17 now genuinely execute and pass (the other two are the intentional "verify the stock behaviour" halves, which correctly stand down when the mods are present). Also new: a report-only tool that flies the same save on both installations and mechanically compares every ghost engine-flame fingerprint between them, so visual differences a mod introduces are enumerated instead of unseen - its first run confirmed the one comparable engine resolves to ReStock's authored effects on the modded install, exactly as designed. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-testing harness gained its first truly gameplay-shaped rewind scenario: a two-stage rocket whose booster carries its own probe core and parachutes - the classic "auto-chute booster" flight the rewind design names as its critical regression guard. The harness can now author that craft mechanically (the first machine-built craft in the fixture library, with every part position derived from the stock part definitions rather than typed in), forge it into a committed launch-pad fixture through a real game session, and fly the mission: launch, cut throttle, stage low so the booster's chutes arm on separation, and land both stages inside physics range before committing. The scenario asserts that the staging split authors a genuine rewind point - the first flight-authored rewind point the suite has ever exercised; every earlier rewind scenario injected a synthetic one - and that a routine two-stage flight leaves nothing behind: neither stage may surface in Unfinished Flights, and the rewind point must be reaped. Flown green and armed the same day: the reaped-rewind-point check is now a hard gate, proven in both directions (a deliberate impossible window turned the run red once before being reverted). Getting there took four flights whose three failures were all in the test driver, never in Parsek - staged during the climb instead of at the apex, then separated at the apex where the halves fell together and collided, then committed while the booster was still under canopy - each now a documented trap for future two-stage lanes. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-testing harness gained the opposite gameplay-shaped rewind scenario to the auto-chute booster above, plus a controlled experiment built on it. A two-part stack is parked in a stable Kerbin orbit and the player stages: the decoupler fires in orbit, both halves keep flying, and the player stays with the crewed half. What should happen is that the half they LEFT BEHIND shows up in Unfinished Flights so they can go back and fly it, the half they are STILL FLYING does not, and the rewind point survives on disk because that unfinished half is still open - the exact inverse of the routine two-stage flight, where both halves finish and everything is cleaned up. The second scenario adds one thing and nothing else: the player briefly switches to the vessel they just released, changes nothing, and leaves. Reading the code said that glance alone might be enough to drop the released vessel out of Unfinished Flights and let its rewind point be cleaned up - which would silently cost the player the ability to go back and fly it - while the rewind design document says a briefly-nudged probe should stay in the list. The two scenarios are deliberately identical apart from that one switch, so the pair measures which is true rather than arguing about it. Both have now flown, and the measurement settled it: without the glance, the left-behind vessel appears in Unfinished Flights and its rewind point survives (that check is armed as a hard gate, proven in both directions); with the glance, the vessel silently vanishes from the list and the rewind point is deleted - one click, no control input, and the player loses the go-back affordance. The measured mechanism is sharper than the prediction: the brief switch leaves behind a small continuation record, and the bookkeeping that decides what counts as unfinished examines that record instead of the vessel's own flight - so the real flight is never considered at all. That finding has since been fixed as a code change - see the Unfinished Flights entry under Fixes below - and the nudge scenario re-flew green against the corrected behaviour and is now the fix's armed regression guard: its window inverted to assert the rewind point SURVIVES the glance, proven in both directions the same day. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated test scenarios can now be run by asking for them by type. There are three types - the everyday set, the long full set, and a small set of expensive ones that only ever run when specifically asked for - and one command flies exactly one of them and leaves a single line saying how it went. It handles what goes wrong when nobody is watching the screen: it holds the computer awake for the whole run (a multi-hour set left alone otherwise gets suspended a couple of minutes in, mid-flight), and if the machine is already busy - another run in progress, or the game open for real work - it steps aside and says who has it rather than queueing behind it, which would have littered the results folder with dozens of records for a run that never flew. When the game installation the tests fly turns out to be out of date, it says so and stops; it never re-installs anything by itself, because which build of Parsek gets tested is a decision a person makes. A failing test is likewise reported and left alone, never quietly re-run until it passes. Afterwards, one line per run says green, red, needs-attention or skipped, with the verdict counts - and a test the harness had to kill for running over budget is always named explicitly so it cannot hide behind twenty passes beside it. The whole routine for asking, running and reading the result is written down, including what accumulates on disk and what is safe to delete. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.

- The Missions tab's rows now match how you count your ships. The old view rendered every structural segment of a vessel as a deeper indent - a three-stage flight read as a staircase of repeated names, and the number of rows never matched the number of craft. Now each physical vessel (and each kerbal on EVA) is ONE row, indented only under the vessel it separated from, with its whole story inline on the row: "Launch → Decoupled (Kerbal X Booster) → Docked (Munport Station) → Landed", its full time span, and how it ended - a same-tree dock names its partner right on the row, and hovering the row shows the full event chain plus what is aboard the vessel ("pod x1, crew x2"), so the composition the old rows printed inline stays one hover away in every interface mode. The per-segment include checkboxes did not go away - expanding a vessel's row (Advanced interface) reveals its segments as flat sub-rows with the same independent checkboxes as before, and the vessel row itself gains a one-click include over all of that vessel's own segments (a partially-included vessel says "(partial)", and clicking it first COMPLETES the selection rather than destroying a hand-trimmed one; a second click excludes it all). Turning on a partner-journey checkbox that silently switched off another mission's loop now announces which mission lost it, same as the Loop toggle does. Nothing about what a checkbox MEANS changed: segment choices stay independent, and dropping a vessel never drags along the pieces that separated from it. Presentation and selection-affordance only: no recording, playback, loop or save behaviour changes.

- Missions window playtest follow-ups (first in-game pass of the new view): the per-mission "#" number and its sortable header now show in the simple interface too - hiding them there made the first column read as a rendering gap rather than a simplification; a row whose text wraps to a second line no longer crops the wrapped text at the top and bottom (the layout measured the cell's height before it knew the cell's width, so a wrapping row got a rect roughly a line short and the centered text clipped at both ends; the cell now feeds its measured width back into the height calculation, and single-line rows are unchanged); and the "Clone" button is now Advanced-only - a clone exists to carry a second loop selection over the same recordings, all controls the simple interface hides, so there it could only create an inert duplicate row. "Delete" stays in both modes so a duplicate made in Advanced can still be removed (the tree's last mission can never be deleted).

- The Missions tab now says what each mission IS, at a glance. Every mission's dark header bar carries a second line telling the mission's story - where it went ("Kerbin → Mun → Kerbin"), how long it took, who flew (crew named, up to three, "+N" for the rest), how it finished, how often it loops, and when it launches next - so a collapsed mission no longer reads as a bare name and eight buttons. The facts the narrative dropped (exact start and end dates, the vessel count, the full roster) sit in the line's hover text, and a mission whose journey cannot be derived falls back to showing its dates. The countdown column, previously the three-letter "TTL", now reads "Next launch", and the countdown also appears on that summary line, so you can see a mission's schedule without expanding it. Inside the mission, the rows read as a story instead of an inventory: a stage that comes off is now named on the row that follows it ("after decouple: Kerbal X Booster left") rather than repeating the ship's name a third time, and docking with another ship recorded in the same mission finally names it - "Docked with Munport Station" - instead of silently growing the part counts. Hovering explains the controls that used to explain nothing: the row checkbox now says that it chooses what the LOOP replays and does NOT hide the ghost (which is what everyone assumed it did), the loop period says which of its four states you are looking at, and the two schedule words "not aligned" and "continuous" say what they mean. Turning on one mission's loop, which can switch off another's because one recording tree can only loop once, now says so on screen and names the mission that lost it, instead of quietly unticking a box on a row you may not be looking at. The cross-tree row is now labelled "Docked partner:" rather than "Partner journey -". Presentation only: no recording, playback, loop or save behaviour changes.

### Settings

- The Settings window got a lot smaller. Nine options that no longer earned their
  place were removed or hardwired:
  - Always on now, toggle deleted: the one-time pre-Parsek save backup, the
    committed-future overlays in the stock R&D / Astronaut Complex / Mission
    Control screens, and the click-blocks that stop you from repeating an action a
    committed mission already performed (double-spending its reserved funds or
    science).
  - Hardwired ON for players, toggle hidden: the three auto-record switches
    (launch, EVA, first modification after switch) and auto-merge - recording and
    committing everything is the mod's premise. The fields survive because the
    automated-testing harness pins them per-run through its command seam.
  - Landing-body alignment is fixed at Loose (~monthly relaunch alignment, a
    few-km handoff seam); the Off / Precise A/B knob is gone.
  - "Force faithful loop playback (no re-aim)" left the window too; the harness
    A/B lanes still set it through the command seam.
  Old saves that stored a different value for one of the hidden switches (e.g.
  `autoMerge = False` from an earlier release) are clamped back to the shipping
  values on load, so what the window shows and what the mod does can no longer
  disagree. What remains: Basic/Advanced, the auto-launch loop period, ghost
  audio, route lines on the map, the Diagnostics section, sample density, and the
  wipe buttons.

- Finished missions now go onto the timeline on their own. "Auto-merge recordings"
  ships ON, so leaving a flight no longer opens the "Merge to Timeline / Discard"
  confirmation dialog for every mission you fly - the recording is simply committed,
  the way it would have been if you had clicked Merge. (As of the settings
  simplification above, auto-merge is permanently on for players - the toggle is
  gone from Settings and the stock difficulty tab, and a career that stored
  `autoMerge = False` from an earlier session is clamped back to ON on load.)
  The reason it stayed off until now was that the automatic path used to be lossy:
  it committed the mission ghost-only and threw away the vessel's final state, so a
  craft you left alive in orbit or on a surface never re-appeared as a real vessel at
  the end of its recording. That was fixed earlier this release - the automatic
  commit now runs the same full-fidelity path the dialog's Merge button always ran,
  keeping surviving vessels spawnable - and this flips the default over to it. Two
  dialogs deliberately stay: a Re-Fly (Rewind-to-Separation) exit still asks, because
  it can supersede history rather than add to it, and quitting to the main menu with
  an uncommitted mission still asks.

### Fixes

- The reputation a kerbal's death costs you is now a real entry on your career timeline, filed against the flight that caused it - so re-flying that flight away takes the penalty away with the death. Losing a crewed craft costs about ten reputation in stock, and Parsek recorded that it happened but never wrote it down as something the career timeline owns. Two things followed from that. On an ordinary flight Parsek's rebuilt career came out ten reputation higher than your real one, so any recalculation that reached your career pool quietly put the penalty back. And on a re-flight merge the penalty was silently handed back - your kerbal's death was undone and so was its cost, but only by accident, with nothing recording that either had happened. The penalty is now written down when the flight is filed, using the exact amount the game took rather than a guessed one - and where nothing captured that amount, no entry is invented. It travels with the death: a merge that retires the death retires the penalty in the same sweep, and a re-flight is not blocked or forced to seal itself over a consequence the merge is about to remove.

- Each death penalty entry now remembers whether it was written down before Parsek had taken your career's starting reputation figure, so a death that is already part of that figure is never charged for twice. The starting figure is read off your live career the first time Parsek files a flight, which can be after a crash has already lowered it; the entry for that crash is marked as already inside the figure and is not subtracted a second time, while a death filed against a figure that was taken earlier is applied normally. The mark is settled once, when the entry is written, and never by comparing moments on the game clock - which is what makes it hold across a rewind, since rewinding winds that clock backwards and a death can carry a later reading than the moment your starting figure was taken and still have happened first, or the other way round. Flights you filed before this change are left exactly as they were: no penalty entry is added to them after the fact, and only flights filed from now on get one. One honest limitation follows from the same rule: because the starting figure is read the first time a flight is filed, a death inside that very first filed flight is already baked into it, so re-flying that one death away does not hand the reputation back. Every later death does. And if the starting figure ends up being taken from career start rather than from your live career, penalty entries written before that are charged normally: they are re-marked the moment that figure is settled, so a death is never written off against a figure that never contained it.

- Money, science and crew experience you earn DURING a re-flight are no longer taken away when you merge it. This is the other half of the rewind-payout fix below, and it needed a different remedy. Recovering a craft partway through a re-flight should credit the new attempt, which is the flight you keep - but Parsek works out which flight a recovery belongs to by asking which recorded flights were running at that moment, and both were: the new attempt, which starts at the rewind point, and the original flight, which ran past it to its own end. With two flights covering the same instant the tie went to whichever ran longer - and until the re-flight overtakes where the original ended, that is the original. So the payout was filed against the flight being replaced, and merging retired it. Keeping payouts stamped before the rewind cannot help here, because this one genuinely happened after it. The tie is now broken in favour of the re-flight in progress, which is the flight that survives the merge, so the refund, the Space-Centre science and the crew experience from that recovery all stay - and they stay together, because all three are filed the same way and are retired as one bundle. Nothing changes when no re-flight is in progress, and a re-flight that has not yet flown anywhere cannot claim a payout.

- Money and science you earned BEFORE a rewind are no longer taken away when you merge the re-flight. Re-flying a mission is supposed to retire only the part of the timeline it replaces - everything from the rewind point onward - but the step that retired it went by which flight a payout was filed against rather than by when the payout happened. The launch you rewound to is one flight from start to finish, so a contract completed or a craft recovered in the first half of it was filed against exactly the same flight as everything after the rewind, and the merge retired the lot. That could quietly undo payment for something that still happened in your career. Parsek now keeps any career entry stamped before the rewind point, using the same cut-off the re-flight already uses when it splits the original flight into a kept half and a replaced half, so the two halves agree on where the seam is. A crew member lost before the rewind stays lost too, along with the reputation it cost - those had been at risk of being undone in the same sweep. Nothing changes for what happened during the re-flight itself, which is still retired as before.

- A craft that a rescue or resupply mission docked with no longer risks reappearing as a duplicate at the space centre. When a docking absorbs a craft Parsek had recorded earlier, that craft's own record is told not to put it back on the pad - it is inside the merged vessel now. The check that did the telling was reading the docking partner's identity from Parsek's cargo-route bookkeeping, which only fills in when the dock also qualifies as a supply route, and a dock with a craft Parsek itself had placed in the world never qualified: a placed craft carries a fresh identity number that check does not recognise. So exactly the craft most likely to reappear out of thin air was the one the safeguard skipped. It now reads the docking partner recorded on the docking event itself, which is filled in for every dock regardless of cargo. Grabbing something with a claw while on EVA still counts as no dock at all, as before.

- A dropped stage or probe whose flight was recorded only in the "relative to its parent" form is no longer deleted as empty. Parsek stores this kind of trajectory twice - once as a position relative to the craft it came off, and once as a plain position over the planet, which is the form the map and the replay actually draw. The tidy-up pass that removes recordings containing no flight data only knew how to look at the first of the two, so a recording with a perfectly good drawable trajectory in the second form looked empty to it and was thrown away - the exact recordings the recorder had just declared worth keeping. Both the tidy-up and the re-flight merge now count the drawable form as real data, on the same two-sample rule the replay itself uses (a single position cannot be drawn as motion, so one sample still counts as nothing).

- Watch mode can no longer keep running with nothing to point the camera at. When a repeating mission starts its next lap, Parsek throws the old ghost away and rebuilds it - and for that instant the camera was still aimed at the discarded one. Aiming a camera at something the game has already deleted is a state KSP does not survive: it throws an error on every single frame from then to the end of the flight, which is exactly what an automated test flight measured, over three hundred of them in a second and a quarter, starting on the very frame the lap turned over. Two things now prevent it. The camera is moved onto a neutral marker parked exactly where the ghost was, a moment before the ghost is deleted, so it is never left holding a deleted object and the view does not jump; and if the camera cannot be re-aimed at the rebuilt ghost after all, watch mode now gives up after a few frames and hands the view back to your own craft instead of staying switched on forever with nothing bound to it. That second guard existed already for one of the two ways this can happen and skipped the other - the missing half is what let a broken watch session outlive the flight rather than end after three frames. One trade worth naming: that path previously waited forever, and now stops after three frames, a figure inherited from the guard that already existed rather than measured for this case - so a genuine camera hiccup lasting longer than three frames would now drop you out of watch mode where before it would have been ridden out. The whole thing was then flown for real on the same test flight that had measured the problem: where that flight used to throw over three hundred errors during play, it now throws none, the camera stays attached to the replay across the lap change, and watching continues normally to the end of the flight.

- The Watch button no longer tells you a ghost is "on a different body" when it is on the same one. Parsek decides which body a ghost is at by remembering where it last drew it, and it only updates that memory while the ghost is close enough to draw - so a ghost too far away keeps answering with wherever it happened to be when it first appeared, however long ago. Standing 144 km from your own replay, in orbit of the same moon, you were told it was on a different body: the replay was at Minmus, you were at Minmus, and the stale note behind the message said Kerbin. It now says the ghost is too far away to be drawn right now, and that getting closer brings the button back, which is what is actually happening. Whether watch mode should be offered at all at that distance was deliberately left alone at the time and has since been fixed too - see the next entry.

- The Watch button now works within the 300 km its own tooltip promises. Standing in orbit of a moon, 144 km from your own replay of the flight that got you there, pressing Watch did nothing: Parsek turned it down because it thought the replay was at a different planet. It was not - it was right there beside you. Parsek works out which body a ghost is at by remembering where it last drew it, and it stops updating that memory once the ghost is too far away to draw, so a distant ghost keeps answering with wherever it happened to be when it first appeared. On a flight from Kerbin to Minmus that first appearance is at Kerbin, and the note stayed at Kerbin for the whole replay. Parsek now works out where the ghost is from the flight it recorded, rather than from that stale note, so a replay that really is beside you is accepted. A replay genuinely at another planet is still turned down, which is what that check is for: the camera has no sensible frame of reference for somewhere millions of kilometres away. Distance is still limited separately, at 300 km, unchanged. One related surprise is gone with it: pressing Watch on a repeating mission used to restart the replay from its beginning - useful when you are standing at the launch pad where it began, but if you are waiting at the destination that beginning is a whole planet away, so the camera jumped there and immediately gave up for being out of range. When the replay is already beside you, it is now simply watched where it is. A related mix-up went with it: while you were watching one repeating flight, Parsek worked out where every OTHER repeating flight in the list currently was using the watched one's schedule instead of their own, so the Watch buttons beside them - and the key that cycles between them - could answer for the wrong moment of those flights, and on a flight that crosses between planets that means the wrong planet. Each row is now read against its own schedule.

- The experience your crew earns from a recovered flight is now recorded in your career history, so re-flying that mission takes it back. Parsek watched the game hand out that experience and wrote down what happened, but it filed the note without saying which flight it belonged to - and a note that belongs to no flight can never be undone by re-flying one. So it deliberately kept the note and recorded nothing in the career history, on the grounds that a permanent entry nothing could reverse would be worse than a missing one. It now works out which recorded flight the recovery belongs to, exactly the way the recovery's refund and its science already do, and files the experience against that flight - which means re-flying the mission retires the experience along with the refund and the science, all together, rather than leaving your crew credited for a flight that no longer happened. A recovery Parsek cannot match to a recorded flight is still left uncredited rather than filed loose. Recovering a craft with several crew aboard now records every one of them, where an earlier version of this would have kept only the first.

- Recovering a craft you have flown more than once now credits the right flight. Parsek decides which recorded flight a recovery belongs to - and therefore which flight gives back the refund, the science and the crew experience if you ever re-fly it - from the craft's name and the time it came home. That is enough when a name has only ever flown once, but a second launch of the same craft carries the same name, so an earlier flight still on record could win the match ahead of the one you actually recovered. Parsek now also checks the identity the game gives a craft the moment it leaves the pad, which is different for every launch, and discards any candidate flight that is provably a different launch before the timing rules are applied. It only ever removes candidates, never adds or reorders one, so a recovery that already matched correctly cannot start matching wrongly - and a flight recorded before Parsek tracked that identity, or a recovery where the game supplies none, falls back to name and time exactly as before. This matters most for crew experience, which unlike the refund and the science cannot be revised once it has been filed against the wrong flight. One deliberate consequence worth knowing about: a craft you place in the world with Real Spawn Control is a copy, and the game gives every copy its own launch identity, so recovering one no longer files its refund or its crew's experience against the original craft's recorded mission - it is credited to no flight at all, which is the honest answer for a craft that never flew that mission. Not yet flown: a two-launch test flight is owed before the second half of this - refusing to guess at all when the remaining candidates are genuinely ambiguous - is built.

- Reputation paid out by a strategy is now recorded in your career history. Strategies like Open-Source Tech Program quietly hand you reputation as a side effect of something else you did - transmitting science, recovering a craft - and Parsek watched that happen and then wrote nothing down, so its reconstruction of your career drifted a little further from the game's own figure with every payout. It is recorded now, using the game's own reputation curve, so the two stay in step.

- Reputation a strategy takes from you is now recorded too, which fixes a drift on any career running Fundraising Campaign or Unpaid Research Program. Those strategies work by skimming a share of every reputation award you earn and turning it into funds or science, and Parsek was writing down the award you were promised while the game handed you the smaller amount that was left after the skim - so its reconstruction of your career ran steadily ahead of the game's own reputation. Measured on a career running Fundraising Campaign at its default commitment, a 20-point contract award lost a full point of reputation that nothing recorded. Parsek had been leaving it out on the reasoning that some other part of it must already be watching the transaction; it turned out the game applies the award and the skim as two separate steps, and nothing was watching the second one. Both are recorded now, as two entries, which is exactly how the game does it.

- Funds a strategy skims from your income are now recorded in your career history too. Appreciation Campaign and Outsourced R&D work by taking a share of every contract payout and milestone award and turning it into reputation or science, and Leadership Initiative scales those same payouts up or down - and Parsek was writing down the payout you were promised while the game credited you the modified amount, so its reconstruction of your funds drifted further from the game's own figure with every contract. Measured on a career running Appreciation Campaign at its default commitment, a 100,000-fund contract reward quietly lost 5,000 funds that nothing recorded, and Outsourced R&D lost 12,500 out of 250,000. Parsek had been leaving all of it out on the reasoning that whatever recorded the payout must already have seen the modified figure; that turns out to be true for launch costs and part purchases, where it watches your balance move, and false for contract rewards, advances and milestone awards, where it writes down the amount the contract or milestone was configured to pay. It now records the skim - or the bonus - alongside the payout on exactly those three, and still leaves the others alone.

- The one-time safety backup Parsek makes of an existing save now recognises more careers as "already played". Parsek only skips that backup for a save it can positively identify as brand new and untouched, and one of the things it looks for is whether any mission milestone has been completed. It was reading only one of the three ways the game records a completed milestone, so a career whose milestones were all reached with a crew aboard - which is most of them - looked to Parsek as though it had completed none. A long-played career could therefore be mistaken for a fresh one and skip its backup, if it also happened to have no craft in flight, no gathered science and no active contracts. All three spellings are now read, along with the achievements the game files underneath each world rather than at the top level.

- Reputation awards now reconstruct at their full value instead of landing fractionally short. The game does not simply add a reputation award to your total - it hands out the award one point at a time, shrinking each point as your reputation climbs, and then tops the total back up by whatever that shrinking cost. Parsek copied the handing-out but not the top-up, and worked out the size of the top-up in a way that came to exactly nothing whenever the award was a whole number - which every mission milestone is. So a pair of +1 record-breaking awards was reconstructed as 1.9985 where the game itself had 2, and the further your reputation was from zero the wider the gap grew: a 50-point award at middling reputation came out at 24 instead of 36. Parsek now sizes the top-up the way the game does, from what the awards actually delivered rather than from what they were nominally worth. Two independently recorded careers that had each been reconstructing reputation slightly low now match the game's own figure to within rounding.

- Recovering a craft now records the refund in your career history. Parsek asked the game up front how much the recovery would be worth, but the game has not worked that figure out yet at the moment it is asked - so the answer was always zero, and Parsek read that zero as "this recovery pays nothing" and dropped the credit for a recovery the game then paid in full. It now recognises a figure the game has not filled in yet and waits for the actual payment instead, and asks again once the sum is finished. A recovery that genuinely pays nothing is still recorded as paying nothing.

- A career whose first contact with Parsek is a flight now records the science and reputation it started with, not just the funds. Parsek waits for the game to finish loading your three career balances before writing down what the career began at, but the wait was over as soon as any ONE of them had loaded - and on the flight route funds always arrive first, so science and reputation were recorded as starting from zero. By the time anything noticed, the flight had already earned science and it was too late to safely take a starting figure, so the zero stuck. The wait now requires all three, and no longer runs before the game has begun loading them.

- Science credited in the opening moments of a scene is no longer missed. Parsek spots a change in funds, science or reputation by comparing against the total it read when the scene loaded - and when the game had not finished loading that total yet, there was nothing to compare against, so the first real change was quietly used as the starting point instead of being recorded. Recovering a craft carrying an experiment landed exactly there: the science was credited to you correctly, but Parsek's record of it lost the note saying where it came from, filed it as transmitted rather than recovered, and the career self-check then reported an error looking for a transmission that never happened. Those totals are now read as soon as the game provides them.

- Two places that quietly edited an existing career row now announce the edit, so nothing downstream keeps answering from the version before it. Parsek keeps short-lived answers to questions like "has this flight already changed the world?" and "what does the career look like right now?", and throws them away whenever the career record changes - but two edits were not counted as changes. One is the moment a fresh launch claims the build cost the game charged a few seconds earlier, which moves that charge onto the flight; the other is a one-time repair of a starting-funds figure that was recorded as zero because the game had not finished loading. Neither had caused a reported problem, but a third case of exactly the same shape had just made a correctly-recorded strategy payout look like a missing one, so all three were closed together.

- Currency traded by an Administration strategy is no longer forgotten. Strategies move one currency into another in two quite different ways, and Parsek was only watching one of them. A one-off sale such as Research Rights Sell-Out was recorded on the money side but not the research side, so the career reconstruction credited you with science you had already spent. A standing cut such as Patents Licensing, which quietly takes a share of every science award and hands back funds, was invisible on both sides: the science it took looked like science you still had, and the funds it paid were too small to notice. Parsek now records the science and the money moved by both kinds of exchange as they happen, and no longer briefly disagrees with the game about your balances while an exchange is going through. Reputation traded by a strategy is still not recorded, because the game applies its own curve to reputation after the trade and the figure available at that moment is not the one your reputation actually moved by. Careers played before this update keep the older, incomplete record for exchanges that already happened.

- A career that sold research through an Administration strategy BEFORE the fix above no longer produces a warning on every single career recalculation. Parsek keeps a standing allowance for the gap between the game taking your science for a trade and the matching career entry being written, because on a live flight that entry is only written when the flight is saved - which can be an hour later. On a career whose trade happened before Parsek learned to record the research side, the game's note of the trade is in the save but the career entry it is waiting for is never coming, so the allowance stayed open forever. On such a career the same thing then happened on every recalculation: the safety check that protects your real balance caught the discrepancy, put your science straight back, and wrote a warning saying so. Your science was never actually wrong - the safety check did its job every time - but the warning repeated endlessly and the log filled up with it. Parsek now measures, once when the career loads, how much of that outstanding amount can never be settled, and stops waiting for that part of it.
