Crucially it only stops waiting to the extent the allowance is not doing real work: on a career where the missing entry genuinely leaves Parsek's reconstruction sitting above your actual science, that allowance is exactly what keeps the two in step, and it is left alone - dropping it there would have produced the same endless warning in the opposite direction, complete with an on-screen message. A trade still in progress on a flight you have not saved yet is untouched and gets its full allowance as before, and a career already recording both sides correctly measures nothing and behaves exactly as before.

- Science recovered from a returning craft keeps its flight attribution while a Patents Licensing style strategy is running. Those strategies leave a trailing zero-value echo behind each award, and the echo was clearing the note Parsek uses to tell a recovery apart from a transmission - so recovered research was filed as transmitted and lost its link to the flight that collected it. The echo is now ignored.

- Switching the interface from Advanced to Basic now shrinks the Settings window to fit, instead of leaving a band of empty space below the buttons. Basic hides the Diagnostics and Sample Density sections, and the window was already asking to be re-fitted when the mode changed - but the re-fit could only ever make the window TALLER. The measurement hands the window's current size to the game's layout pass, and that pass only ever grows a window to fit its content - handed a window that is already taller than it needs to be, it leaves it exactly as it is. So it did. Going the other way, Basic to Advanced, hid the problem completely: that direction needs the window to grow, which is the half that worked. The measurement now hands over no height at all, which leaves the layout pass with one answer to give - the height the content actually needs - so both directions fit. The window's position and width are untouched, as before.

- A career payout is no longer credited to a flight that has stopped existing. When you rewind to re-fly a moment, Parsek opens a provisional recording for the new attempt, and until you merge it that recording is not part of your history yet. Two different things wear that state and they needed opposite handling, which is the heart of this fix. A payout you earn DURING a live re-fly - recovering a craft partway through the new attempt - genuinely belongs to that attempt, and is still credited to it exactly as before: the attempt becomes your real timeline when you merge, so the credit becomes real along with it. What was wrong is the leftovers. An abandoned attempt from an earlier session sits in the save waiting to be swept away, and because it carries the name of the craft it came from and is the newest thing on the books, anything asking "which flight does this recovery belong to?" picked THAT one. When the sweep then removed it, the recovery funds and Space-Centre science were left pointing at a flight that no longer existed. The lookup now tells the two apart by identity rather than by state, so a live attempt keeps its credit and a leftover is passed over in favour of a real committed flight. Where the only match is a leftover, the payout is left uncredited rather than pinned to something doomed. Rows already mis-filed in existing saves are not rewritten by this; they are now reported instead (see below).

- Re-fly attempts that end without being merged now hand their career rows back properly, instead of leaving them labelled with a deleted flight. Both ways an attempt can end - Parsek concluding one that produced nothing, and you choosing Discard - removed the recording and its files but left any funds or science earned during the attempt still labelled with that recording's name. That label is not decoration: it is what Parsek reads at merge time to decide which career rows belong to a timeline being replaced, so a label pointing at a deleted flight could later be swept into a different merge and a REAL payout cancelled out. Both paths now clear the label and keep the row, so the money and science stay exactly where they are while the dead reference goes away. Nothing you have earned changes as a result of this - it removes a way it could have been wrongly taken back later.

- A replay whose flight path is stored in sections rather than as a plain list of points can no longer be thrown away as empty. Parsek's tidy-up pass removes recordings that hold nothing playable, and it decided that by looking at three places a path can live - while some recordings legitimately keep theirs in a fourth. Those read as having no data at all and were eligible for deletion, even though the merge step that decides what your timeline keeps looked at that fourth place and correctly considered them worth keeping. The two now agree on this point, so a tidy-up can no longer delete a recording the merge would have kept. A recording that genuinely holds nothing is still removed exactly as before, and the existing safety net that already refused to delete a recording a live rewind session still owed something for stays in place as a second line of defence.

- Replays and rewinds no longer mistake a fresh launch of the same design for the craft they recorded. The game stamps a craft file with an identifying number and hands the SAME number to every launch of that design, so a rocket you launch today carries the number your recordings of that rocket carry from weeks ago. That was harmless while a rewind emptied the world of everything but the craft you went back to; now that a rewind leaves the rest of your program flying, a second Kerbal X parked in orbit answers to the recorded one's number, and several parts of Parsek believed it. The worst of them was silent and permanent: while recording a docking or a close formation, Parsek stores the moving craft's position relative to its partner, and it picked its partner by that shared number - so with the wrong same-design craft in the scene it wrote a whole approach measured against a craft on the other side of the planet, and the replay of that flight was quietly wrong forever with nothing to hint at it. The same mix-up hid replays that should have been visible (a ghost is skipped when "its own craft is already in the world", and the stranger looked like it), retired a replay's map presence while its own craft was nowhere in the scene, ended a piece of debris' recording early because it thought the craft it fell off had gone on rails, and left a recording marked as already-materialised against a craft it never spawned, which permanently blocked the replay from putting its own craft back. Every one of those decisions now also checks the game's per-launch identity, which is genuinely unique per launch and is never stored in the craft file: a design number match still counts, but a conclusive per-launch mismatch never does. Recordings made before Parsek tracked that identity are unaffected and behave exactly as they did - an unknown identity is not treated as a mismatch. One place deliberately still goes by the design number alone, and the code says why: the check that stops a craft you rewound from re-appearing beside the re-flight you are flying, where the re-flight IS a fresh launch of the same design by definition, so reading the per-launch identity there would resurrect the duplicate that check exists to prevent. That decision now writes a line into the log whenever it holds a craft back, so the case where it holds one back for the wrong reason is diagnosable rather than silent.

- Going back to re-fly a separation is now steadier about the world it lands in, in three ways that only started mattering once a rewind stopped clearing your program out of the sky. First: a craft belonging to one of the OTHER craft from that same separation is put away as a replay even when Parsek could not identify it at the time the rewind point was made. Those craft are meant to leave the world and continue as recordings, and one Parsek had failed to pin down at the time was simply skipped - so it stayed in the world as a real craft while its recording ALSO played back over it, which is the doubled-craft problem that confuses the game's own trajectory drawing. Identification for this is strict, by the game's per-launch identity rather than by name, so an unrelated craft of yours that happens to share a name is never touched - and strict here means a POSITIVE identity match rather than merely the absence of a contradiction. That is the opposite of how Parsek reads an unknown identity everywhere else, deliberately: elsewhere an unknown one falls back to what the code did before per-launch identities existed, but here that fallback would end in deleting a craft rather than in leaving one alone, so a craft is only put away when its identity positively matches. A recording too old to carry one leaves its craft in the world instead - the same behaviour you had before this fix, never worse than it. Second: the rewind now waits for the specific craft you chose to actually be in the world before it starts working, rather than for the world to contain anything at all - with your program preserved, "something is loaded" was true several moments before your craft was, and the rewind could start too early and abandon itself with "selected vessel not present". Third: when a crew member cannot be seated in a craft Parsek puts back because that kerbal is aboard something else you still have flying, the log now says which craft is holding them, and says plainly when it has emptied every seat. That is the correct outcome - a kerbal is one person and cannot be in two places - but it looks like a Parsek fault from the outside, so it is now legible instead of silent.

- Kerbal experience now survives a rewind correctly: a crew member whose flight the rewind leaves alone keeps what they earned, and one whose flight the rewind replaces does not. Experience is not a number the game stores - it is worked out from a log of what each kerbal has done, written when they are brought home. Going back to re-fly a moment restores that log to how it stood then, so every entry filed since is erased, including entries filed by crews on completely unrelated flights. Those kerbals silently lost levels they had earned, sometimes dropping a rank, and nothing put it back. Parsek now records what each returning crew member's log gained, and after a rewind it puts back the entries belonging to flights that still stand. It only ever ADDS: entries the game legitimately dropped stay dropped, and a kerbal whose flight was replaced by the re-fly correctly does not get theirs back - they have to earn it again on the new attempt. The put-back now happens the moment you finish a re-fly, rather than waiting for whatever unrelated thing next made Parsek recalculate - so a crew's levels are right as soon as you are back in the world, and right in the save written straight after. Anything a kerbal did before Parsek was installed, or on a flight it never recorded, is untouched. Experience is also only ever recorded for a recovery YOU performed: Parsek recovers craft of its own accord in a few housekeeping situations (clearing a duplicate left by a quickload, tidying up craft it had put in the world itself), and those no longer hand out career experience for a homecoming that never happened.

- A craft that a rewind puts back in flight no longer leaves you holding its recovery payout as well. Going back to re-fly a moment restores the world as it stood then, which brings back craft you had recovered since - they are flying again, exactly as they were. Their recovery funds, their recovery science and their crew's "safely home" status all stayed on the books, so you had the craft AND the money for having brought it home, and there was no way to give either back. Parsek now retires those rewards at the moment you confirm the rewind, in the same breath as putting the craft back. Only the rewards of a recovery that happened AFTER the rewind point are touched - anything you brought home before it was never undone and is left alone. Science the craft TRANSMITTED while it was flying is left alone too: you had that the moment it was sent, whether or not the craft ever came home, so only the science the recovery itself paid out is taken back. The rewind confirmation now says so before you commit to it. Identification is strict on purpose: a craft only counts as the same one when the game's own per-launch identity matches, so a fresh launch of the same design can never be mistaken for the craft coming back and have its rewards taken. Nothing is deleted from your history - the recovery is marked retired, the same way a re-fly retires the flight it replaces.

- A contract that comes back after you go back and re-fly a moment now keeps the progress it had at that moment, instead of resetting to the day you accepted it. Re-flying a stretch of a mission undoes whatever that stretch did to your career, and a contract it finished or failed is put back on your active list. Parsek rebuilt it from the only copy it had kept, which was taken the instant you accepted the contract - so a survey contract you had already ticked off eleven of twelve sites for came back showing zero of twelve, and there was no way to get those back other than flying them again. Parsek now also takes a copy of every active contract at the moment a rewind point is made, and rebuilds from that one: the contract returns exactly as it stood when the timeline rewound. The old copy is still kept and is still what gets used for a contract that no rewind touched, so nothing that worked before changes. Copies are thrown away along with the rewind point they belong to, so this does not grow your save over a long career.

- Science you earned after a rewind point, on a flight the rewind did not touch, no longer vanishes from the Science Archive and no longer lets you collect it twice. Going back to re-fly a moment restores the research building to how it stood at that moment, which wipes out every experiment result first filed after it - including results filed by a completely different craft whose flight the rewind leaves alone. Parsek's own ledger knew those results were still earned and tried to put them back, but it could only correct entries the research building already had a row for, and a result first filed after the rewind point has no row to correct: the correction was silently counted as "not found" and skipped. The archive then under-reported that experiment for good, and the damage did not stop there - re-running the experiment paid out in full a second time, because as far as the game was concerned it had never been run, while the ledger only credited what was still owed. The difference stuck, because the safety check that stops a rewind from wrongly draining your science reads the game's number as the truthful one whenever the ledger's is lower. Parsek now creates the missing archive entry rather than skipping it, so the experiment is back in the archive with the exact total you earned, and re-running it pays what a partly-completed experiment should. The entry is created with placeholder labels the game fills in properly the first time you run that experiment again, and it is only ever created for a result the ledger actually credits - a rewind that legitimately un-earns an experiment still leaves it out of the archive.
- A booster you have already staged away no longer keeps writing its engine into the recording of the craft it left behind. Parsek works out which engines and thrusters a craft has once, when it starts recording, and then reads those same engines every frame. It only ever checked whether a part had been blown up - and a jettisoned booster is not blown up, it becomes its own piece of debris and often keeps burning for another twenty or thirty seconds. So for as long as it burned, its ignitions, throttle changes and final shutdown were filed against the craft that dropped it, and the replay of that craft showed a plume coming from an engine that was no longer attached to it. Parsek now checks each frame that an engine, thruster or robotic part still belongs to the craft being recorded, and quietly stops reading it once it does not - the booster's own recording, which does exist, is where its burn belongs. The same check now runs on craft Parsek is watching in the background, where the identical mix-up was possible. The list of engines and thrusters is also rebuilt whenever the game reports the craft's shape changed - staging, decoupling, docking or undocking - which fixes the other half of the same problem: a part welded on during a construction EVA, or an engine that arrived with a craft you docked to, was never in the list Parsek built at the start and so recorded nothing at all for the rest of the flight. Rebuilding also forgets the parts that left, which closes a quieter half of the same problem: because Parsek had stopped reading the jettisoned booster, it never saw that engine stop, so it still believed it was running - and when the flight ended it dutifully wrote a "shut down" for it, minutes later, into the recording of the craft that had dropped it. That late entry counted as real activity, which meant a long quiet coast at the end of a flight could no longer be trimmed away as boring. Both are gone now. An engine on a part that stayed is untouched by the rebuild, so one that was already burning is still known to be burning and nothing flickers at the moment a stage separates; a part that only momentarily looks absent, as happens during a docking shuffle, is not forgotten either, and what the booster was doing when it came off is still handed to the booster's own recording. On balance this records less, not more: what it adds is confined to engines and thrusters that genuinely arrived on the craft, and what it removes is a whole burn's worth of misfiled events plus the stale shutdown that was keeping boring tails alive.

- A craft Parsek is watching in the background no longer freezes mid-burn when you warp away from it. When you leave a craft's neighbourhood the game puts it "on rails" - it stops simulating it part by part and just moves it along its orbit. The craft you are actually flying has always been told to shut its plumes off at that moment; a background craft was not, so a booster that was still burning when you warped away replayed with its engine lit for the entire warp, however long that was, and its thrusters stuck on with it. Background craft now get the same shutdown the flown craft gets. The other half of the same problem was worse and quieter: when the craft came back off rails, Parsek re-checked every panel, lamp, bay door, chute and engine against the real craft and quietly agreed with whatever it now found - without writing any of it down. So anything that changed while it was away was not merely recorded late, it was erased: a chute that deployed, a panel that folded, an engine that was still running when you came back, all silently absorbed and never replayed. Parsek now remembers what the craft looked like when it went on rails and, when it comes back, records the difference - typically two to four events per round trip, and nothing at all when nothing changed.

- Four things that were supposed to be recorded, and were listed as recorded, turned out never to have been recorded on a real craft at all - they are now. The glow of a heat shield on re-entry is the big one: replays have always had the code to show a shield glowing orange and cooling back down, and it had never once been fed a real number, because the value it was looking for is not one the game exposes under that name. Re-entry now looks like re-entry in a replay. Airbrakes and deploying flaps are the second: whether a control surface was out was checked against a name no stock part has, so a spaceplane that dropped its airbrakes on approach replayed with them tucked flat, every time. Rover suspension is the third - the number Parsek read was a fixed setting from the part's config file that never changes, so a rover bouncing over Mun boulders recorded a perfectly still suspension; it now reads the real travel. Robot pistons are the fourth, and were the funniest: the value being recorded as "how far the piston is extended" was actually the piston's SPEED SETTING, which does not move during a stroke, so a crane extending its arm recorded nothing while its speed slider was faithfully preserved. All four were found by reading the game's own code rather than by guessing at names, and each fix says in a comment which field it is reading and why. Older recordings are unaffected - none of this can be recovered after the fact - but everything recorded from here on carries it.
- A Re-Fly you start and then end without actually flying now finishes on the spot, instead of leaving the mission in a state that only sorts itself out the next time you load. It showed up only if you saved or loaded between going back and ending the session - a quicksave, a quickload, anything that reloads while a Re-Fly is open - which is common enough to be worth naming. What happened then: the re-flight's own (empty) record was tidied away as having nothing in it, and the step that closes out the session went looking for it, could not find it, and gave up with a warning; the mission was left carrying a dangling re-fly marker that the next load noticed, complained about, and cleaned up. The end result was always correct - your original branch stayed the real one, nothing was overwritten, nothing was lost - but the route there was an accident, and an accident is not something you want load-bearing. Two things changed. The tidy-up now refuses to throw away a re-flight that actually recorded something, and when the re-flight really is empty it hands it to the closing-out step instead of deleting it behind that step's back. And the closing-out step now reaches the decision it was always meant to reach: it runs the same check that decides whether a re-flight replaces the branch you went back from, gets the same answer it would have got anyway (an empty re-flight replaces nothing), and closes the session there and then - no warning, no dangling marker, no next-load cleanup. That matters beyond tidiness, because the same step is what settles a replaced branch's books, undoing the reputation hits and crew losses an abandoned timeline caused. On this particular ending there is nothing to settle, since nothing was flown - but it was being skipped by accident rather than reached and decided, and now it is always reached and decided. The rewind point itself is left exactly where it was, so the separation stays as re-flyable as it was before you tried.

- Replayed craft now appear the way they actually looked, instead of the way they looked in the parts catalogue. A ghost was built from a saved copy of the craft, and that copy has always recorded which panels were out, which gear was down, which bay doors were open, which lamps were lit and where every robot arm was pointing - but none of it was read. The ghost was assembled at each part's default pose and then corrected by the flight's own recorded events, so anything the recording never had an event for stayed at the default: a rover with its arm already unfolded replayed folded flat, a lander that came off its parent with legs down replayed with legs up, a lamp left on came back dark. Whatever the saved craft says is now applied as the ghost's starting look, and wherever the flight recorded a change to one of those things, its own record takes over from there - so a replay that used to start wrong and stay wrong now starts right, and one that started wrong and was corrected a few seconds in no longer flickers through the wrong look first. Where a flight recorded nothing at all about something, the saved craft is what stands, which is the right answer for anything that did not change while it was being recorded. This also fixes the case where a flight was picked up again mid-mission (switching to a craft you left in orbit, or continuing after a docking): those stretches begin with the craft already configured and record no starting-state changes of their own, so nothing existed to correct their replay's defaults - the saved copy of the craft is now what supplies it. Older recordings that only kept a copy of the craft as it looked at the END of the flight are deliberately left out of this: starting a replay from how a flight finished would be its own kind of wrong (a chute cut on landing would be missing for the whole descent), so those keep their old starting look and only their shape comes from the saved copy.

- Robotic parts on a replayed flight no longer snap back to their resting pose at the point where the flight was cut in two, or at the moment a looped replay starts over. Going back and re-flying a moment splits the flight record at that moment, and everything after the cut is replayed as its own stretch - so whatever state the craft was already in has to be carried across. Panels, gear, bay doors, lamps and chutes were carried across, but only when they were OPEN, out, down or lit; hinges, rotation servos and pistons were not carried at all. Both halves of that are fixed here. Carrying only the open direction used to be harmless, because a stretch after a cut began with everything shut anyway - but now that a replay starts from the way the craft was actually saved, "shut" has to be stated too, or a plane that raised its gear during the climb would fly the rest of its ascent with the gear still down. A rover that had already unfolded its arm, or a crane holding a load at half extension, replayed the whole stretch after the cut with the arm folded flat as though it had never moved, and because that stretch often contains no further servo movement at all, it never recovered. Servo poses now cross the cut the way the other reversible states do: one pose per servo, the pose it was actually in at that moment, with each servo on a part carried separately; a servo caught mid-swing is put where it was and picks its motion back up from the recording's own later samples. Reading a servo's pose out of the saved craft also had to be taught which numbers a saved craft actually contains: a hinge or rotation servo is placed at the angle it was commanded to, a piston at the extension it was commanded to, and a helicopter rotor is left alone entirely - nothing the game saves says how fast a rotor was actually turning, only what speed it was allowed to reach, so a parked helicopter would otherwise have replayed with its rotors at full speed from the first frame and spun up again every time a looped replay came round. The same pose was also being inherited the wrong way round on a loop: every other visual state was reset for the next cycle, but servos were left standing wherever the last cycle finished, so cycle two of a rover replay began with the arm already out. Each cycle now restarts every servo from the same pose the first one did.
- A parachute you repack on EVA no longer replays as an empty can for the rest of the flight. Cut a chute, walk a kerbal over, repack it, and the replay showed the pack sitting there with its nose cone gone and nothing inside - permanently, on every viewing, and it never self-corrected. The recording was at fault rather than the replay: Parsek tracked only three chute states and folded "packed", "armed" and "cut away" together into one, so repacking - which in the game means going from cut back to packed - looked exactly like cutting, and got written down as a cut. The replay then did faithfully what a cut asks for, which includes blowing off the nose cone with nothing that ever puts it back. Chutes are now tracked in four states, so repacking is recorded as its own thing and the replay restores the packed look, nose cone included, exactly as the game does on the real craft. This is fixed on both sides of the recorder, and the second one matters more than it sounds: repacking is done by a kerbal standing outside, which means the kerbal is who you are flying and the craft being repacked is one Parsek is watching in the background - the likelier of the two paths, and the one a fix to only the obvious half would have missed. A chute that is already cut when a recording begins is handled too: it no longer produces a phantom cut at the start of the segment, and a repack after that is still noticed. Chutes that were repacked in already-recorded flights stay as they were recorded; the fix applies from here on. The packed look also now survives a flight being cut in two - going back and re-flying a moment splits the record there, and the stretch after the cut is told outright that the chute is packed rather than being left to infer it. That distinction did not used to exist: a stretch after a cut began from the parts catalogue's own resting look, which for a chute happens to BE the packed look, so nothing needed saying. Now that a replay starts from how the craft was actually saved, a chute that deployed early in a flight and was repacked later would otherwise have hung open for the whole second half.

- Rover wheels now turn because the rover is moving, which is not what they were doing before. Three things were visibly wrong at once: a rover coasting downhill or gliding to a stop showed completely motionless wheels; driving in reverse looked identical to driving forwards; and when the wheels did turn, the speed they turned at meant nothing in particular. All three had the same cause. The recorder was reading the one wheel number the game makes available, which is not a rotation speed at all - it is the percentage of maximum turning force the motor is currently applying, always positive, and zero whenever you are not actively driving. That number was then replayed as though it were a rotation speed. Hence stationary wheels while coasting (no motor input, so zero), reverse looking like forwards (the number has no sign), and meaningless rates. Parsek now stores nothing at all for wheel spin and works it out during playback from how fast the replayed craft is actually travelling across the ground, divided by the wheel's own radius taken from the part - so coasting turns the wheels, reversing turns them backwards, and the rate matches the speed. Wheels only turn while the craft is actually on the ground, which matters most for the case that is easy to overlook: a rover riding a rocket up to orbit is moving at two kilometres a second, and reading the spin off that speed would have had its wheels blurring for the whole ascent and the whole coast. They now stop the moment the craft leaves the ground and start again when it comes back down - which is, in passing, also how a plane's wheels behave across a takeoff and a landing. Because the spin is derived from the movement rather than read from the recording, it also fixes flights that were already recorded, and it makes recordings slightly smaller rather than larger.

- The two recording fixes above now have checks that run inside the game, which matters because one of them could not be checked any other way. Working out how fast a wheel should turn is arithmetic that can be checked on a desk; working out which WAY it turns depends on a piece of the game engine's own maths that only exists while the game is running, so until now that one step was reasoned about rather than verified - and getting it backwards would have meant every rover in every replay driving forwards with its wheels spinning in reverse. There is now a check that runs it for real and says so. Two more join it: one builds a parachute from the actual game part, cuts it and repacks it, and confirms the nose cone comes off and goes back on; the other builds a real rover wheel and confirms it turns while the craft is driving, stops when it is parked, and stops when the craft is off the ground. Two new demonstration recordings were added to the test save to go with them - a chute being cut and repacked on a loop, and a rover actually driving across the ground rather than sitting still. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change beyond the two fixes above.
- Rewinding to a separation point no longer deletes the rest of your space program. Until now, invoking a Re-Fly removed every real vessel from the loaded game except the one you were going back to re-fly: your stations, relay satellites, rovers and landers, every deployed science cluster, every flag you had planted, and - worst of the set, because these cannot be replaced - every asteroid and comet you had discovered and were tracking, including ones an active contract was pointing at. Nothing was said, nothing was recoverable, and the career economy kept crediting recoveries and contract completions for a fleet that no longer existed. What made it hard to spot is that both layers doing the deleting looked deliberate: a pre-load pass rewrote the quicksave down to the single selected craft, and the post-load pass was then told to strip anything it could not match. It was also self-concealing - the code that exists specifically to spare planted flags could never fire, because the flags had already been removed from the save file before it was consulted. Both layers now do what the design always specified: a vessel that belongs to this rewind point's own set of craft is still put away (that is the mechanism by which the rest of your stack becomes a replay), and a vessel that has nothing to do with the rewind is left exactly where it was. The narrow, name-matched removal of prior-career debris that would otherwise confuse stock trajectory prediction is a separate mechanism and is untouched - it still runs, so the problem that motivated the wide deletion stays fixed. Two other things come back to life with it: the flag exemption now actually protects flags, and a long-dormant warning that tells you when a left-behind craft shares its name with one of your recordings is reachable for the first time. A preserved craft's own controls are also no longer touched - only the craft you are re-flying gets its throttle closed, which is unchanged. Keeping your fleet also required fixing two things that were only harmless while the fleet was being deleted, and both would have been worse than the original bug. First, an existing cleanup pass that removes leftover debris which would otherwise confuse the game's own trajectory prediction identifies its targets purely by matching craft NAMES - and it had been dormant ever since the wide deletion arrived, because from that day on it only ever ran in a world containing exactly one craft. It was not always dormant: the day before, a playtest caught it clearing three pieces of leftover debris, and all three were craft the game itself classified as debris. Turned loose on a preserved fleet it would have deleted real craft: the game names every launch of a design identically, so a station or lander that happens to share the name of the craft you are re-flying was eligible, and it is removed silently with no entry in your career records. It is now restricted to craft the game actually classifies as debris, which is what it was always described as doing - and which is exactly what that one observed clearance consisted of, so the only removal this pass has ever been seen to make still happens. Second, the bookkeeping that decides whether a recording's replay craft still exists was comparing only the internal craft ID that the game bakes into a saved design and reuses on every launch - so a fresh launch of the same rocket, now preserved instead of deleted, would be mistaken for the replay and that replay would never appear again. It now compares the per-launch identity as well, which the rest of the mod already does elsewhere. Also hardened while in here: the check that a Re-Fly found the craft it was sent to find now looks for that craft specifically instead of merely counting survivors, so a rewind point whose target has gone missing refuses cleanly rather than silently starting you on whichever unrelated vessel happened to be first in the file.

- Ten in-game self-tests that reported "passed" while checking nothing - or could not check what they claimed to - now say what they actually did. (Two of the ten turn out to have been honest already: one was correctly skipping and was left alone, one really does run its checks and only had its wording aligned.) A per-test read of the self-test suite found cells that ran, went green, and asserted over an empty collection or bailed out early through a silent early-return - a test that cannot fail is worse than no test, because it reads as coverage. Each one is now honest: where the required context is missing (no ghost map vessels, an empty crew-replacement list, a sandbox save that exercises none of the money/science/reputation checks) the cell reports SKIPPED and names both what it needed and how to produce it, instead of a green tick. Two got real checks rather than only honesty: the ghost-ID collision walk now records how many real craft it compared against how many ghosts and fails if that was none, and the session-start log-format check now validates the line the game actually writes - it used to build its own copy of that line and check that against itself, so it could never have caught the format drifting. A cell whose PASS becomes a SKIP looks like a step backwards in the tallies and is a step forwards in truth: the number of tests that really executed did not change, only the honesty of what is reported. The automated flights that check all this were then re-flown to record the new counts, and they turned up something nobody expected: two of the map-presence checks had never been exercising anything even on the automated flight that was specifically set up to give them something to check. That setup was believed to work and had never been measured; it does not. The flight now reports those two as skipped, which is the truth, and the numbers moved accordingly. Giving them something real to check is written down as follow-up work. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.

- Glancing at a vessel you left behind no longer makes it disappear from Unfinished Flights. Deploy a probe in orbit, click across to it on the map to see how it is doing, change nothing, and go back to what you were flying: until now that single look silently removed the probe from the Unfinished Flights list and deleted the rewind point behind it, so the option to go back and actually fly the probe was gone, with nothing said and nothing to undo. Not looking kept both. Two things were wrong. Switching onto a vessel that Parsek was tracking in the background closed off its flight without recording how that flight stood - the only way a flight could be closed without that being written down - and separately, the bookkeeping that decides what counts as unfinished treated the small continuation record your look creates as if the vessel had been handed off to something else, and stopped looking at the vessel's own flight. Both are fixed: a flight is never closed without its state being recorded, and a continuation created purely by switching is now understood as the same vessel continuing, so the vessel's real outcome is read through it. A genuine hand-off - docking, an EVA, a decoupler - is still a hand-off and behaves as before. Your probe stays in the list and stays re-flyable, and you close the row yourself with Seal when you are done with it, which is how it was always meant to work.
- An automated crew-loss test flight can no longer call a craft that never left the pad "landed with crew alive". The mission's survival verdict checked that the craft was down and the crew alive, but nothing checked that a flight had actually happened - so a pod sitting on the launch pad with its crew aboard satisfied it within two seconds. The verdict now also requires the craft to have been SEEN leaving the ground (either an observed in-flight state on two consecutive readings, or a 100 m climb over its own first pad reading) before it may conclude; readings that arrive blind because of a telemetry fault neither count toward that nor erase it, and a flight that provably never left the ground is now named as such instead of timing out anonymously. Verified against the recorded telemetry of both the false alarm and the real passing flights, and then re-flown for real: the flight passes exactly as before, and its readings confirm that on this test's own setup the survival verdict never had a usable view of the craft at all - it has always been decided by the crew roster, which is why the new requirement reports what it saw rather than being allowed to block a pass. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The synthetic test flight used to verify crew-death bookkeeping across a rewind no longer carries a second copy of its crew member in the root of the flight history. That duplicate held its own indefinite claim on the kerbal, so the test could never demonstrate that tombstoning the death releases the crew slot - the very thing one coverage cell exists to prove. While fixing it, the test's own "this vessel carries no crew" checks turned out to be incapable of failing (they searched compressed binary files as if they were text); they now decode the files first and prove they decoded the right vessel before asserting, and the fixed check was demonstrated to catch the old fixture. The re-fly that fix made possible then ran, and settled the question: the duplicate claim was indeed the cause, and the release works. It also showed the check everyone expected to use was backwards - a released crew slot is exactly what CREATES the stand-in that check would have banned, so the obvious test would have passed only while the bookkeeping did nothing. The developer log line that reports the recomputed crew claims now also says how many of them are permanent (a death) versus temporary (a kerbal still out on a mission), which is what actually distinguishes the two cases, and the automated test now checks that instead - confirmed on a further flight, which read exactly that line and passed. Test-tooling and developer logging only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-testing harness no longer benches a healthy test scenario because of a problem with the machine it ran on. The harness tracks how often each scenario fails for reasons unrelated to what it is testing, and permanently quarantines one that fails too often - a deliberate one-way door, since a scenario that cannot be trusted should stay out of the nightly run until a human looks at it. But failures that happen before the game even starts - a missing Python environment, or another run already holding the machine - are properties of the machine, not of the scenario that happened to be queued at that moment, and they were counting against it. One such failure was enough to quarantine a scenario forever, and because these failures arrive in batches, a single run holding the machine could have benched most of the suite in one go. They are now excluded from the calculation entirely; genuine instability in a scenario still counts exactly as before, and nothing already quarantined is released automatically. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer log no longer reports a bogus internal-cleanup failure on every re-fly that continues the same vessel. The merge that concludes a re-fly walks the flight's history looking for leftovers from an earlier abandoned attempt, and it warned whenever it found an uncommitted flight record where it expected none. Because a re-fly that continues the same vessel gives its new record the same vessel identity as the one it continues, the walk kept finding the *current* re-fly's own record - which is supposed to be there, is not a leftover, and must never be cleaned up while the re-fly is still running. The walk now recognises the running session's own record and passes over it quietly, so the warning is back to meaning what it says: a genuine leftover from a previous abandoned attempt. Diagnostics only - the re-fly itself, and everything it supersedes, behaved correctly throughout.
- Archiving a flight no longer removes it from the Timeline for good. The Archive checkbox lives in the recordings list, which Basic mode hides, so a flight archived in Advanced vanished from the Timeline with no way back. The Timeline's filter bar now has its own "Archived" button that brings archived flights back, marked "[archived]", in both modes; it is the same Archive filter the recordings list uses, and the Timeline still hides archived flights by default, exactly as before.
- After a merge that could not seal a Re-Fly slot, the message now points at the Timeline, where the Seal button actually is and which is visible in every UI mode.
- A kerbal who dies when their vessel is destroyed is now correctly recorded as dead on the career timeline. Previously the crew-fate step was skipped for destroyed vessels (the only flights that end with no vessel left to snapshot), so a dead crew member was treated like one still away on a mission: their seat got a temporary reservation and a stand-in kerbal was generated, instead of the permanent reservation a death is supposed to leave behind.
- Predicted flight tails and orbit-propagated ghost positions now keep their real orientation. The trajectory segments Parsek predicts when a falling vessel leaves the scene were saved with their orbit angles in radians while everything that draws or replays them expects degrees, and the reverse mix-up made the predictor and the ghost endpoint placement read recorded degree values as radians, so predicted map orbits and propagated ghost positions could point in essentially arbitrary directions. Newly recorded orbit segments now use one unit convention end to end; predicted segments already saved by older versions are left as they are.
- Parsek now predicts the right crash site for a vessel you leave falling. When you leave the scene mid-descent, Parsek finishes the flight by predicting where the vessel ends up - and to know when it hits the ground it has to ask the planet how high the terrain is under it. It was asking about the wrong place: the position it handed over used a different axis convention than the one the game answers in, which swapped two of the three axes and moved the question tens of degrees of latitude away. The ground height it got back - and with it the moment the predicted flight ends - therefore belonged to somewhere else entirely, and the error is largest on bodies with dramatic relief, like the Mun. The same axis mix-up also displaced the handover when a predicted flight crossed from one body's influence into another's, and left a predicted tail's ghost pointing the wrong way when it replayed. All of it is now measured rather than assumed: a self-test flown in the running game reported that the prediction code placed an equatorial vessel at 34 degrees north, and a second reported a predicted ghost's orientation off by 133 degrees. A confirmation flight then showed the position fix exact - the same self-test now reproduces a live vessel's latitude and longitude to six decimals - while the orientation was still off by 131 degrees, so that half got a second look rather than a second guess. The cause turned out to be that the predictor works out where a craft is from its orbit's shape and tilt using textbook mathematics, while the game measures one of those angles from a slightly different starting direction, leaving every predicted position and speed spun about the planet's axis relative to what playback expects. The predictor now converts into the game's own convention before recording an orientation, and the whole chain is pinned by a headless reconstruction of the game's own orbit mathematics, so this no longer needs a test flight to diagnose. A second confirmation flight then closed it: both self-tests read zero. The position one still reproduces the live vessel's latitude and longitude to six decimals, and the orientation one now comes back matching the vessel's own exactly, rather than merely closely enough to pass. Both stand as regression guards. Predicted segments already saved by older versions keep their old orientation, as with the earlier unit fix.
- A flight tail predicted from an ALREADY-SAVED orbit now lands in the right place, and a predicted orbit Parsek writes down now replays the right way round. The previous fix corrected the one place the in-game measurement was taken; the same mismatch was present throughout the code that predicts a tail, and this closes it at that code's own source rather than one seam at a time. One further place that reads a saved orbit by another route - the ghost-position extender - is knowingly not covered and is recorded as still owing the same treatment. The game measures one of an orbit's angles - the one that says where the orbit's tilt starts - from its own fixed direction in space, not from the bare mathematical axis a textbook propagation uses, and the two differ by a fixed rotation about the planet's axis (measured at 230 degrees in the running game). Parsek's propagator was reading a saved orbit's angles as if they were textbook ones, so anything it worked out from a SAVED orbit came out spun about the planet's axis: a tail finished from a saved orbit rather than from the live craft ended up at the wrong longitude, and any orbit the predictor wrote back out was replayed spun the other way. Height, altitude and latitude were never affected, which is why nothing that depends on altitude ever looked wrong. The conversion now happens once, at the single point where the propagator reads and writes those saved angles, so the two ways Parsek can start a prediction - from a saved orbit, or from the live craft - agree with each other and with the crash-site fix above, and the local patch the previous fix needed has been removed rather than left to double up. The game turns that reference direction as the planet turns, about a degree a minute, so the conversion is worked out afresh each time rather than remembered - the whole prediction is finished within a single frame, so both ends of it use the same reading, and what gets written down does not depend on when it was written. Predicted orbits already saved by older versions keep their old angles and will show the difference, as with the two fixes above; nothing is rewritten. A second, separate weakness the same investigation found - the propagator's solver losing accuracy on very stretched orbits - is deliberately not touched here and is fixed next.
- Parsek's orbit predictor now solves very stretched orbits the way the game itself does, instead of losing its way on them. Working out where a craft is along its orbit at a given moment means solving an equation that has no direct answer, so it is solved by repeated approximation - and the standard method for that quietly stops working on strongly stretched orbits, near the point of closest approach. The game knows this and switches to a sturdier method past a certain stretch; Parsek's predictor did not, and kept using the standard one everywhere. That mattered far more than it sounds, because the most stretched orbit in the game is the one every craft sitting on the ground is technically on - so the case the predictor handled worst was the most common one there is. On that orbit the old method could finish its allowance of attempts still more than a hundred degrees away from the answer. Parsek now makes the same switch at the same point and uses the game's own two methods on either side of it, so a predicted position agrees with the game's to the last decimal at every stretch and every point along the orbit, rather than only on gentle orbits. One deliberate difference: the game's gentler method is allowed to keep trying forever, which Parsek cannot afford - this code runs before every recorded sample, so a run that never ended would cost the recording rather than just the answer. It is given a generous limit, after which it returns its best answer and says so in the log. Nothing that can actually happen in game reaches that limit; it exists so that if something ever does, it is loud instead of silent.
- A ghost replaying an orbit now holds the attitude it was actually recorded with. To replay how a craft was pointing, Parsek stores its orientation relative to the direction it was travelling; the recorder has always written that down using the craft's real-world direction of travel, but the replay code read the direction of travel from the game's orbit maths, which reports it along a different set of axes than everything else in the game uses. One orientation frame was therefore being built out of two different frames, so every orbiting ghost was replayed turned - by 79 degrees on a worked example. This affects EVERY recording ever made, since almost all of them contain orbit stretches, and it is a change you will SEE: ghosts that used to coast sideways or upside-down through their orbits now hold the attitude the flight actually had. Nothing on disk is rewritten and no recording is invalidated - only the reading of it is corrected. Three producers moved onto the recorder's convention at the same time so nothing is left half-converted: the predictor that finishes a tail after you leave the scene, the same predictor's handover when a predicted tail crosses into another planet's sphere of influence (which was silently turning the ghost at every crossing), and the two duplicated copies of the replay maths that re-place ghosts after the game shifts its floating origin. Predicted tails written down by earlier versions carry the old convention and will replay turned, exactly as with the two orbit-angle fixes above; new ones are written the new way.
- Added a self-test that measures the fix above against a live craft, because the existing orbit-attitude self-test structurally cannot see it: that one runs Parsek's predictor against Parsek's replay code, so a mistake shared by both cancels inside it and it reads a perfect zero either way. The new one starts from the RECORDER's own orientation capture - which is pinned to the game's own reporting and cannot be quietly moved to match a wrong reader - and requires it to come back out of the replay code as the craft's real attitude. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- An EVA in orbit is now recorded. A kerbal floating free in orbit can put Kerbal Space Program's own trajectory predictor into a state where it hands back numbers that are not numbers at all, and Parsek's recorder hit that on every single physics frame - which took the whole frame down with it, before any of the recording work for that frame had happened. A ten-second orbital EVA therefore finished with one point and nothing else: no path on the map, no ghost to replay, and no sign on screen that anything had gone wrong. Parsek now recognises an unusable prediction, keeps the last good one and carries on recording, refuses to store such a prediction in a recording at all, and reports it once in the log instead of once per frame. A failure while preparing a prediction can no longer cost the recording a sample, whatever its cause.
- Concluding a Re-Fly that never flew (rewind, then end the session without launching) no longer leaves the save stuck part-way through the merge and failing on every later load. The merge now completes with nothing superseded, which is the correct outcome when there is no new flight to replace the original with.
- If a Re-Fly attempt ends up with nothing recording into it, Parsek now says so on screen and in the log at the moment it happens, instead of the attempt silently failing to replace the original at merge time.
- Leaving the flight scene during a Re-Fly attempt without moving the craft off the pad now shows the merge-or-discard prompt instead of silently throwing the attempt away. The idle-on-pad cleanup that discards a recording nobody flew was firing on a live Re-Fly attempt too, which left the session with nothing to conclude: no prompt appeared, the attempt never merged and never discarded, and its placeholder stayed in the save indefinitely.
- Launching a second copy of the same craft in one session no longer corrupts the first craft's recording: the reload's recording-resume now refuses to adopt a freshly rolled-out vessel (or any vessel from a different launch), so the new flight gets its own recording instead of writing its events into the previous vessel's.
- The plain go-back rewind (Rewind to Launch / warp back) now reconciles supply routes the same way a Re-Fly rewind does: routes created after the rewind target go dormant instead of continuing to run before their own creation point, and surviving routes correctly re-deliver re-played cycles instead of silently skipping them.
- After a rewind, surviving supply routes now restore their timeline-correct paused or active state, their completed and skipped cycle counters, and drop any armed Send Once or pause-after-cycle one-shot; a Send Once route recovering from a crash mid-delivery also pauses correctly now instead of staying active and sending a second cycle.
- Science gathered after a rewind point is no longer paid out when that timeline is undone by a Re-Fly: experiment results captured between the rewind point and the rewind itself are now discarded with the rest of the abandoned future, instead of being silently credited at the merge for an experiment that never happened on the surviving timeline.
- With Auto-merge recordings turned on (Settings), a vessel you leave surviving at the end of a mission (in orbit, landed, or splashed) now stays a real, controllable vessel on the timeline instead of becoming a visual-only ghost, and landed or splashed missions no longer interrupt with a confirmation prompt. (Closing that gap is what allowed Auto-merge to become the default later in this same release - see Settings, above.)
- New recordings no longer store two overlapping trajectory sections for the same time span around time-warp seams, which made the ghost's playback position ambiguous in those windows. Existing recordings are left untouched.
- A flight that ends in a crash before its recording is committed no longer saves overlapping trajectory sections at each booster-separation boundary; the recorder now closes and reopens sections at the exact same instant, so crashed-flight saves pass the same integrity checks as surviving flights.
- Supply-route inventory delivery now uses every cargo container on the destination vessel: when the first container is full, items are delivered into the next container with a free slot instead of being reported as undelivered. Pickup already worked this way; delivery now matches it.
- Supply-route inventory deliveries now deliver the full stacked quantity of a cargo item to a loaded destination instead of a single unit, and a manifest item is split across as many inventory slots as its stack size requires (one slot per unit for non-stackable items) so the delivered inventory is valid stock state on both the loaded and unloaded paths.
- Supply-route inventory deliveries now respect the containers' packed-volume and mass limits, summed across every cargo container on the destination: an item that would not fit is skipped as not-fitting at planning time on both the loaded and unloaded paths, instead of being written into a container that would refuse it.
- A kerbal who goes EVA and climbs straight back in without moving is now recorded as boarding again: the mission tree gets its board merge point and the EVA leg ends as "boarded" instead of the kerbal's recording being dropped as destroyed. If the mission tree is already left pointing at another recording by an earlier failed start, the board merge is skipped rather than overwriting it, so no recording is lost either way.
- The career-earnings self-check no longer reports a false problem every time a kerbal dies. It was looking for the reputation hit under a stock reason code that does not exist, so the reputation KSP actually deducted for the loss was never matched up and the check logged a warning about a missing earning channel on every crew death.
- Facility upgrades are now recorded on the career timeline the moment they happen, instead of only being noticed on the next scene change. An upgrade done and then followed by a quit or reload without changing scene was previously missed entirely; it is now captured immediately for both the stock upgrade UI and the developer test path.
- A failed write no longer destroys the file it was replacing. When the game could not write one of Parsek's files - a full disk, a permissions problem, or the file held open by a backup tool or virus scanner - the previous version was deleted before the failure was noticed, so the data was lost with nothing written in its place; this covered recordings, the career ledger, the settings file, milestones and the game-state store. Parsek now confirms the new file actually landed before touching the existing one, and puts it in place with a single swap instead of a delete followed by a rename, so an interrupted write leaves the previous file intact and the game keeps loading what it had. On the rare systems where that single swap is unavailable, the previous file is set aside under a uniquely-named copy and put back if anything goes wrong, with its name written to the log.
- Saving while Parsek is holding a restored mission tree open no longer leaves stray recording files behind. When one recording in the in-flight tree cannot be written yet (it belongs to history Parsek must not overwrite before you confirm a merge), the whole tree is deliberately skipped for that save - but any other recording in the same tree had already had its data files written, leaving files on disk that nothing referenced. Parsek now decides whether the tree can be saved before writing any of its files, so either the tree and its files are all saved, or none of them are.
- A kerbal who is re-flown and then brought home is released again instead of staying booked out forever. Parsek decides what became of each crew member - still aboard, recovered, lost - once, from the flight's own outcome, and only a recovered kerbal is ever handed back with an end date. A re-fly's new flight record, though, is handed its craft at the moment you rewind, before it has any outcome, so the very next bookkeeping pass settled every crew member as "outcome not known" and then treated that as final for the life of the record. That answer books the kerbal out indefinitely. It made no difference for a re-fly that ends in orbit or on the ground, which books the kerbal out the same way, but a re-fly that ends in recovery never got to say so: the kerbal stayed reserved, kept generating stand-ins, and never returned to the roster. The verdict is now retired whenever a flight's outcome is written down, so the next pass re-reads it against the real ending. The same correction covers a flight that lands and is only recovered later from the space centre, and one whose outcome is overridden to destroyed - both had the same stale-verdict problem from a different direction. A verdict is only ever dropped when Parsek can re-derive it, so nothing is lost on records it could not re-read.

- Every Parsek window now carries a help box just above its Close button, showing the help text for whatever control you are pointing at. It is always there and always exactly two lines tall, empty when you are hovering nothing, so a window no longer changes height and its bottom row no longer shuffles as the pointer crosses a button or a cell. Previously the box appeared and disappeared with the pointer, flashed a dark sliver across the window bottom on the way in, and sat above the Close button in some windows and below it in others; help text longer than the box now simply stops at two lines. The Real Spawn Control window had a worse version of the same fault: hovering "Warp to Next Spawn" threw a layout error every frame, which stopped the rest of that window drawing and left its resize corner dead until the pointer moved away. The two test-runner windows also get their boxed help strip back, having been dropped to plain text to hide the flicker. Every help text was then re-edited to actually fit those two lines in its own window - the Settings window, narrow enough that some of its help ran to four lines and lost its ending, now says the same things in one short sentence apiece. The help box has also been added to the windows that never had one - the main Parsek window, Kerbals, Career, Timeline and the Gloops Flight Recorder - and a lot more controls now explain themselves when you point at them: every button on the main window says what its window is for, the Timeline's filter buttons say what they show, the Career tabs say what "pending" means and what a UT column is, and the Kerbals rows say what clicking them does. The Timeline is the clearest gain: it already had written help for most of its filters, and the game had no way of showing you any of it until now. (Two details of this entry were superseded later in the same release: the strip is no longer "always exactly two lines tall" - the widest windows reserve one line and over-long text scrolls instead of stopping, see Features, "The hover-help strips of the widest windows are now ONE line tall"; and the Gloops Flight Recorder window listed here is no longer reachable, see Changed, "The Gloops Flight Recorder button and window are gone from the Parsek UI".)

### Internals & Tests

- A month-old open question about why watch mode refuses at 144 km is closed, without a re-flight. The finding had been written up twice - once with the wrong threshold, once with the wrong mechanism - and ended with three suspects and no way to tell them apart, because the refusal is the failure of a three-part test and the log named only the test, never the part. Reading the code against the archived logs of the four flights that measured it settles it: the part that says no is the same-body check, and it says no because the answer it reads is written once when the ghost first appears and then only refreshed while the ghost is close enough to draw. A ghost too far away keeps its first answer forever - in the flights that measured this, "Kerbin", held for three seconds while both the observer and the replay were at Minmus. A first draft of this write-up said the far ghost had no recorded body at all; the logs it cites contain the line that disproves that, and the corrected version is the one above. The refusal is also not a flat rule about distance: one branch positions a far-away ghost early when its replay has a moment coming up that needs preparing, and that refreshes the answer. The two suspects that were ranked ahead of it are ruled out by the same evidence - the ghost's own frame log prints its distance and its zone on the refusing frame, which is only possible if the ghost exists (suspect one) and if the distance the range test reads was a real number well inside the limit (suspect two, already excluded in writing). The experiment the write-up had specified for a future flight is shipped anyway, because it is worth having permanently and costs nothing: the refusal now prints all three answers per candidate, so any future log names the part that said no instead of requiring this reconstruction. The refusal itself is deliberately not changed - several test flights pin it by name, so moving it is a decision for whoever owns them, not a side effect of diagnosing it. Reporting and documentation only; no behaviour change. (Superseded later the same day: the refusal WAS changed, on this diagnosis - see Fixes, "The Watch button now works within the 300 km its own tooltip promises". The same-body check now resolves the ghost's body from the flight it recorded rather than from the stale drawn-position note this entry identifies, so a replay genuinely beside you is accepted; the 300 km distance limit is untouched.)

- The career bookkeeping fixes above are now proved end to end, by an automated flight rather than by argument. A test flight launches a career craft from the pad, hops, lands, runs three science experiments, transmits them and recovers the craft - and the career it leaves behind is kept as a permanent test case. Replaying that career's recorded history and comparing the result against the game's own saved balances used to come out short on all three counts: money by the whole recovery refund, research by the whole starting balance, reputation by a fraction of a point. It now matches to the limit of what the game's own numbers can express - money exactly, research and reputation to the last digit either side can represent. The previous version of that test case existed to pin the three gaps as exact amounts so the fixes would be provable, and it did its job: each amount is what made its cause findable rather than guessable. It has been replaced by the flight flown on fixed code, and the test rewritten from measuring the gaps to proving there are none. The flight itself also stopped reporting an error it used to log every run, and now runs on the nightly schedule instead of by hand.

- The nine spec comments, across seven test-flight specifications, that had been repeating the mis-quoted arrival number now say what was actually measured. Sizing the Jool flight (above) turned up a piece of folklore the suite had been citing to itself for a month: that the autopilot's course corrections arrive HIGHER than asked for, evidenced by a Mun flight that "turned a 250 km request into 956-1,142 km". Both halves were wrong - those passes were flown at a 60 km request, the top of the band came from a flight on record as a lucky off-axis burn, and the single B5 flight ever flown at 250 km came in at 138.9 km, i.e. short, which is what the underlying finding said in the first place. The nine comments that repeated it are the ones that JUSTIFY where each flight aims, so each was re-derived against the measured record rather than reworded: the Mun lanes now price their capture off the 136-141 km actually delivered at that request (which moves the worst-case fuel figure up, still inside budget); the Eve, Dres, Moho and Eeloo lanes now say that the delivered periapsis tracks a fraction of the destination's sphere of influence rather than a multiple of the request, and each cites its own flown arrival - which is why Dres and Eeloo genuinely do come in far above the request while the Mun does not. Every conclusion survived the correction and not one setting changed value, which is the point worth recording: the parameters were right, the reasons written beside them were not. Two summary lines in the status doc carrying the same shorthand are softened to match. Docs and comments only; no behaviour change, no flight re-flown.

- The automated-testing suite gains a flight to Jool - by far the largest destination it has ever been pointed at - and writing it corrected something the suite had believed about itself for a month. The flight is the same one already flown to Dres, Moho and Eeloo, retargeted: launch, park, drop the spent stages, burn for the planet at its window, coast, correct twice on the way, capture into an orbit and save the recording there. Nine of its fifty-six settings differ from the Eeloo version; the rest are copied. Sizing where to aim meant going back through twenty-five past arrivals across seven destinations - every one whose delivered periapsis could be read from two independent channels - and the result contradicted the program's own written note on the subject. The note said the autopilot's course corrections arrive HIGHER than asked for, and cited a Mun flight that turned a 250 km request into 956-1,142 km. The number is real but it was flown at a 60 km request, not 250 km, and its upper end comes from a flight that is on record as a wild off-axis burn that got lucky - one later re-flown honestly to replace it; the single B5 flight ever flown at 250 km came in at 138.9 km, i.e. LOW - which is what the original finding actually said. Measured across all seven destinations, what the corrector really does is deliver a periapsis that is a fraction of the target's sphere of influence, roughly regardless of the request, so "arrives higher" is an artefact of asking for something tiny relative to that scale, and the bias inverts once the request passes about four percent of the sphere. Jool's request sits at twenty-four percent, deeper into the inverted side than anything ever flown, so the aim is set to the smallest request whose worst measured shortfall still clears Pol's orbit rather than to a deliberately low one. It has now flown, and passed first time: the craft captured into a Jool orbit 590,327,171 m out, circular to nine kilometres, comfortably clear of the outermost moon. The aim was the one real gamble and it came in at 97.4% of what was asked for - which settles the question the sizing turned on, because the best-fitting rule over all past arrivals said the request would barely matter and predicted something six times lower. It matters. Two of the sizing's own pessimisms also turned out wrong in the safe direction: the mid-course corrections cost 197 m/s against 500 assumed, and the capture burn came in at the textbook-optimal figure rather than the third-again-over that the Eeloo flight had suggested was normal. The recording count is now pinned at five off the measurement, with a tenth of the drop-tank fuel still unspent. A second lane now reads that recording back as a repeating mission and checks the schedule it produces. It was deliberately shipped blind first - required to prove only that the machinery ran, with the "it declined" outcomes left permitted, because a lane that fails on its own most interesting result cannot report it. It engaged: the replayed mission re-aims from Kerbin to Jool, and the repeat interval came out at exactly three times the interval between the two planets lining up - the figure predicted in writing beforehand, alongside a lining-up interval predicted to fifteen digits. Flown twice in total - the blind reading run and the armed one - with every measured figure identical run to run. It also adds a fifth data point to how much of a replayed mission is dead waiting time that gets compressed away - and the five together do not fall neatly with journey length, so what looked like a trend across three of them is not one. A third lane jumps the replay clock into the arrival itself, so the part of the machinery that re-plans each individual journey actually runs and can be checked. Four things were predicted in writing before it flew and all four came back exact. It also adds a fourth data point to something the suite can now say properly: the angle the planner's chosen route actually ends up at has no relationship to how tilted the destination is. Two of the four destinations trip the check that handles awkward approach angles every run and two never do, and which side a destination falls on is a property of the route the planner picks rather than of the destination itself - so choosing where to fly by how tilted it is does not control which behaviour gets tested. Worth knowing before anyone flies one hoping it will. Separately, all four of these arrival lanes now also check the SHAPE of the re-planned route, not just where and when it starts and ends: they pinned the two endpoints, the plane and the timing, but nothing about the ellipse in between, so a change to its shape that kept those fixed would have passed every one of them. Narrow, since two ellipses through the same two points at the same times in the same plane cannot differ by much - but real, and cheap to close. The lane was flown blind first, which paid for itself immediately: the arrival instant it had been told to jump to turned out to be thirteen days off the real one, and a single-pass version would have quietly locked in a check that never looks at the arrival at all. A distance check that reads zero at one destination and eighty-four percent of the way out at Jool turned out, on reading all four lanes, to be two different code paths rather than one inconsistent number - the line says which it is using, and only one of them measures what its name suggests. That remaining question - which behaviour is the intended one - is now settled: the coarse path is intended, because its one precision-hungry consumer already sharpens the value itself before using it, so "fixing" the source would change nothing a player sees while invalidating two of the suite's calibrated flights. The contract is now written down at the code sites instead, and the number stays out of the tests permanently because the two paths' readings measure different things and cannot be compared. One judgement call is recorded as refuted rather than quietly kept: the correction budget was raised on the argument that Jool might need it, and the largest correction the flight actually planned was a tenth of that ceiling. The corrected record, and the nine places that were carrying the old citation, are written down - a list produced by grepping for the number rather than from memory, after a first draft of the correction got some of its own attributions wrong and was itself corrected. Those nine have since been corrected as well; see the entry above. Test tooling and docs only; no gameplay change.

- Two diagnostic instruments in the map view stopped crying wolf, and one of them stopped going quiet at the exact moment it was asked a question. Both are developer tools that ship switched off; neither affects normal play. The first watches for a replayed craft's orbit line flickering out and back on the map - a real visual defect worth catching - and it had been reporting one every time a test jumped the clock past the end of a recording. That is not a flicker: past the end of what was recorded there is no path left to draw, so the line going dark is the correct picture, and the watcher was calling a correct transition a fault. Reading all thirteen such reports ever collected showed the same shape arriving from two directions - some caught at the moment the line went out, some one frame later when it came back - so the fix asks the question that actually settles it: at the moment the line went dark, had the replay clock left the stretch of flight the recording covers? Only the one place in the code that measures exactly that is allowed to answer yes, and every other reason a line goes dark still reports as before - hidden while another drawing takes over, hidden below the atmosphere, hidden waiting for a refresh, or gone dark with nothing explaining why. A genuine flicker inside the recorded stretch is untouched, which is the whole point: the check is now sharper, not more forgiving, and a test fails the build if anyone widens it. The second instrument counts how many arrival-geometry checks a frame performed. It shared one five-second cooling-off period between "I measured something" and "I measured nothing", so on a short test flight the first uninteresting frame silenced the interesting one for the rest of the run, and three test lanes had to record their arrival reading as prose instead of a checked number. The two now have separate budgets, so a frame that measured nothing can no longer talk over the frame that did - and all three of those lanes, re-run without changing a thing about what they fly, printed the reading they had been missing and now check it automatically.

- When a looped interplanetary mission declines to re-aim because its transfer got cut in two, the log now says so instead of appearing to blame a missing transfer.
