The machinery that decides whether a replayed mission can be re-aimed at a planet's current position reads one recording at a time, and it needs the whole transfer - parking orbit, the coast between planets, and the arrival - inside that one recording. When the load-time optimizer legitimately cuts a mission in half mid-transfer, no half holds all three, so every half is turned down with the same message: no coast between planets was recorded. That is also exactly what a mission which genuinely never recorded one produces, and the two were indistinguishable - which is why the one real occurrence of this cost a whole diagnostic flight to track down. Now the log re-reads the cut pieces together, as one mission, and only when they add up to a real transfer does it say so: which sibling holds the coast, where the mission was going, and how many pieces it is in - from both sides, so the half holding the parking points forward and the half holding the coast points back. That "only when they add up" is the point of the check rather than a detail: a half-flight that ejects to solar orbit and stops, or a Moon return cut at the same boundary, would each have a piece that looks like the missing coast, and announcing a transfer for either would trade one misleading message for another. Nothing about which missions re-aim changed; only what the log says when one does not. The wording the automated test lanes watch for is preserved verbatim, so their regression guards keep matching. The underlying fragility - that the check wants the whole transfer in one piece - is unchanged and stays recorded as open. Diagnostics only; no gameplay change.

- Follow-ups to the test-asset trim, all three of which needed a machine the previous change did not have. First, the test helper that used to load a frozen copy of an old career is gone rather than merely unreachable: when that fixture was deleted, roughly 230 lines below its entry point became dead code, and they were left in place because excising them could not be compiled where the deletion was made. They were one contiguous block holding nothing else, so removing it plus four call-site edits took out 293 lines with no behaviour change - the count the deleted code contributed was always zero, and the test that exercises it still passes. Two automated-test descriptions elsewhere stated their reason for existing in terms of one of the deleted helpers; they now state the same guarantee in terms of what remains, so the reasoning survives the symbol it used to name. Second, the coverage ledger claimed a storage format that no longer exists: it listed a file type the mod stopped writing, with not one such file anywhere in the project, yet two test scenarios claimed to cover it - a check reporting green on something nothing could exercise. The value and both claims are removed together, since a scenario claiming a value the ledger does not list is rejected outright; all 107 scenarios still validate. Third, the contributor-facing instructions file had drifted from the code on three counts, each checked against the source rather than against the sibling copy: it listed that same retired file type as current, it understated the recording schema generation by one, and it named a stored field by a name that was renamed some time ago (in three places, one of which still described the rename as future work). All four now match what the code actually does. Test assets, tooling and documentation only; no gameplay change.

- The automated-testing fixtures no longer commit the same spacecraft once per test save. Each committed test save needs its craft files in its own ship folder, because that is the folder the automation asks the game to launch from - so as the suite grew, the same designs were copied into save after save. Twelve byte-identical copies of the stock Kerbal X had accumulated, plus seven of one booster and five of one probe: 27 files and roughly 181,000 duplicated lines, which is why recent test-fixture changes have been arriving as pull requests hundreds of thousands of lines long. Each copy was also its own chance to go stale, and the suite had already started paying for that: the tool that authors the Duna probe had grown a list naming "EVERY committed copy of the craft" so its drift check could walk all of them, after a check that watched only one copy stayed green while the copy the nightly run actually flew went out of date. Now each shared craft is committed once, in one library, and copied into the test save as it is staged for a run - so what the game sees at run time is unchanged, byte for byte, verified across all 22 committed saves. A craft used by only one save stays where it is. The safeguards are the point rather than the size: the suite now fingerprints the whole fixture tree and fails if any file is byte-identical to a library craft (including one that was renamed), fails if a library craft drops to a single user, and staging refuses to boot the game at all - naming the craft and the save - if a save asks for a craft the library does not have, or carries a copy of one it also asks for. The save harvester drops a craft the library already holds and prints the line to add instead. Test assets and tooling only; no gameplay change.

- Committed test recordings no longer carry a second, human-readable copy of data the game can rebuild on its own. Parsek writes a readable text version beside each of a recording's three saved files, as a debugging aid - and harvesting a flight into a test fixture brought all of them along, so the test folder held both the compact file the game reads and a text copy four to ten times its size. Two of the three are now left out: 99 files and 334,000 lines, getting on for twice what the shared craft library saved (all three kinds together would have been three times it). Nothing is lost, because those two are rebuilt from the compact files - which are still committed - the next time the recording is saved, so loading the fixture in the game brings the readable copies straight back. The third, the one covering the flight path itself, is deliberately kept, and for a stronger reason than it first appeared: two test suites read those files directly as input, so removing them would break tests outright rather than merely cost a reading aid - and four test descriptions also quote figures out of them. The safeguard checks all three halves - that the readable copies stay out, that the compact files they are rebuilt from stay in, and that the one being quoted survives - so a later tidy-up cannot take the wrong one. The save harvester drops them too, so a future harvest cannot put them back. The readable-copy feature itself is untouched: a real flight still writes all three, exactly as before. Test assets and tooling only; no gameplay change.

- Committed test saves no longer carry three kinds of leftover that arrived with them and that nothing ever reads. Building a test fixture from a real flight copies the produced save wholesale, so whatever the game and the mod happened to write alongside came too. Three such populations were measured and removed: the old "rewind to launch" snapshots, one per recorded mission, at 137,000 lines - no test, no automation step and no health check reads them, only a button a human could press while looking at the save; three leftover quicksaves, each a near-copy of the very save sitting beside it, differing by a few dozen lines; and two empty marker files in a folder whose own rules say nothing should be committed there. The rewind snapshots needed care rather than deletion: each is named by a line inside the save, and removing the file while leaving the line would make the health check report a broken reference - and for one fixture it would have escalated that to a failure and turned an automated run red. File and reference were removed together, and a check now fails if either half is ever reintroduced alone. Two of the things that LOOK like leftovers are not, and are explicitly protected by the same check: the separate rewind-point saves, which are genuinely read, and the readable flight-path copies, which turned out to be a live input to two test suites rather than merely a reading aid. Also repaired: the file listing what git should ignore had text-encoding corruption spliced into it, silently disabling two of its rules; and committed test saves are now pinned to keep their exact line endings, so a contributor whose git is configured to rewrite them no longer fails a stack of byte-for-byte checks for reasons unrelated to their change - without hiding those files from review, which was the tempting shortcut and the wrong one. Across this and the two changes above, the committed test-asset folder falls from 1,226,000 lines to 550,000. Test assets and tooling only; no gameplay change.

- Removed a 74,000-line test fixture that the code had been refusing to load for three months, and closed a hazard hiding underneath it. When the recording format was reset in May, the decision was to reject old recordings outright rather than convert them - and this fixture, a frozen copy of an old career, was on the wrong side of that line. It was marked "excluded until rebaked" and then nobody rebaked it, because the rebake never made sense: the same policy that rejected the old files also forbids reading them, so rebaking always meant flying something new rather than converting this. Something new was duly flown - the automated test suite now holds fifty real recordings from real missions at the current format - and this fixture sat unread ever since, forty of its forty-one files never opened once. Checked carefully before removing it: nothing cites its recordings except one archived note and one test that had already copied the numbers it needed inline, and the one test that mentions it asserts its data is ABSENT, on the branch that has been taken every run since May. The hazard: that code fell back to reading a real career save off the developer's own machine whenever the fixture was missing. Deleting the fixture would have made that fallback the normal path, so a machine with recordings in its default save would have quietly pulled private, unrepeatable data into a test and flipped its result. Both fallbacks are gone; a missing fixture now simply yields nothing. Test assets only; no gameplay change.

- The recording analyzer now reports career rows that are filed against a flight it cannot find, so the rows already mis-filed in existing saves stop being invisible. The fixes above close the ways they were created, but they are prospective - they do not go back and re-file rows already written. The analyzer's ledger check now raises one warning per unknown flight it finds referenced, saying how many rows point at it, and the same check runs inside the game as part of the recording-invariants self-tests. It is a warning rather than a failure on purpose, for two reasons. First, a label pointing at a flight that does not exist ANYWHERE cannot be matched to a timeline being replaced, so unlike a label pointing at the wrong REAL flight it cannot cause a payout to be cancelled - the row still applies and your totals reconcile, making this specific case a filing-cabinet problem rather than a damaged save. Second, a warning cannot turn an automated run red, so surfacing a pre-existing population in every affected save does not manufacture a wall of new failures. A save whose flight list failed to load is skipped, so a corrupt file is reported once by the check that owns it instead of flooding this one. The report format itself is unchanged. Also fixed alongside it: a log line that announced a leaf recording as having "no playback data" was reading the same incomplete set of places as the tidy-up pass above, and so said that about section-stored recordings that actually had data. Diagnostics only in that case; nothing behaved differently.

- The way Parsek decides "is this recording's craft the one in front of me" is now settled in one place, and the deliberate exceptions say why they are exceptions. Several decisions used to answer that by comparing the number the game bakes into a craft file, which every launch of that design shares; each is now either routed through the per-launch identity check that already existed for the same question elsewhere, or carries a written argument for staying as it was. Two stay: the check that stops a rewound craft re-appearing beside the re-flight you are flying (where the re-flight is a fresh launch of the same design, so the identity check would defeat the purpose), and the low-level "does a craft with this number exist" lookup that the identity-aware check is itself built on. The one duplicated-crew decision in the family turned out not to be an identity question at all and is argued from the game's crew roster instead - a kerbal is a single roster entry and cannot be in two places, so removing them from a craft being put back is right, and what was owed was a clearer log line. The unsafe half of the spawn-state reconciler was deleted outright rather than left available, so nothing can pick it by accident, and its tests were moved onto the surviving one. Also centralised: the one-line clean-up that ends a re-fly session now drops its own temporary hand-over note, instead of nine separate places each having to remember. Internal only; covered by 37 new or ported headless test cells.

- A new in-game self-test category checks the fix above against the real game rather than only in the headless suite, and a new automated scenario runs it unattended. The headless tests can prove the saved-craft data is read correctly and that the right decision comes out of it, but they cannot prove anything MOVED: every piece of code that actually poses a panel, a leg or a robot arm reaches into the game engine, and calling one from a headless test aborts before it runs a line. So the question the whole fix turns on - does a saved craft that says "panels out" really put the replay's parts somewhere other than the catalogue's default pose - had no answer outside a running game. Seven new cells answer it: each one builds its own single-part craft description over a part it finds in the live catalogue, then measures where the built replay's parts actually sit. They also check the deliberate non-actions (a panel caught mid-travel is left alone) and the loop restore (a robot arm moved during one cycle is put back for the next). Tolerances scale with distance rather than being fixed, and a cell that cannot find the kind of part it needs - a robot arm needs the Breaking Ground expansion - says so and skips instead of asserting against an assumed install. The scenario that flies them declares up front that its pass/skip split is not yet measured, and its check still fails a run in which nothing actually executed. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The fix that stopped a Re-Fly deleting the rest of your space program can now be proved inside a running game, which is the one thing its existing tests could not do. Every check written for that fix inspects the rewritten save file before the game loads it, or exercises a decision in isolation - and the bug had TWO layers deleting the world, one of them after the load, so "the save file looks right" is exactly what the defect looked like. There is now a set of six in-game self-tests that read the surviving world out of the running game after a Re-Fly has actually been invoked, and compare it against the saved world the Re-Fly came from: nothing unrelated may be missing, the craft from that same separation must be gone, a real craft that happens to share the re-flown craft's name must survive while genuine leftover debris under that name is still cleared, and planted flags and tracked asteroids must specifically still be there. The comparison uses the same code that decides what to remove, so the check cannot drift away from what it is checking, and each test says plainly which precondition it needs and steps aside when a Re-Fly is not in progress rather than passing on nothing. A new automated scenario drives the whole thing unattended - it loads a purpose-built save whose rewind point carries a small fleet (a station, a discovered asteroid, a planted flag, and a probe-and-debris pair deliberately named after the craft being re-flown), invokes the Re-Fly, and runs the six tests while the session is still open. It has not flown yet; its first scheduled run is its proof. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.

- The developer-only stack provisioner no longer refetches pinned source code it already has. The layer that decides how to obtain each pinned source correctly concluded "the cached copy already contains the pinned commit, nothing to fetch" - but the layer that acts on that decision had no branch for it: anything that was not a fresh clone fell into "refetch", so every live provision made two needless round-trips to github.com, and the log contradicted itself, reporting the commit present on one line and "pinned commit missing" on the next. Observed on a live warm-cache provision run on 2026-08-12. A warm cache now resolves both pinned sources with no network traffic of its own (the release-artifact download step is separate and still runs on every live provision), the fetch log line states the real reason a fetch runs (a stale or re-pointed cache, not always a missing commit), and a new test builds a warm cache and proves the reuse path invokes no network operation at all. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.

- The developer-only automated test that dismisses a kerbal now checks the roster it changed, instead of leaning on log lines saying the dismissal ran. It reads the produced save and requires that the dismissed kerbal's name is gone from the roster while the three other original crew names are still listed - a check on the names present, not on their state or type. Both fail the run outright, and a run whose save carries no roster reading at all is reported as a tooling fault rather than quietly passing. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Parsek's independent read of a career save now also sees the kerbal roster, the unlocked tech nodes with the parts each one bought, and the active strategies, so the check that Parsek's reconstruction still agrees with the game's own save file is no longer limited to money, science, reputation, buildings, contracts, milestones and vessels. Three reporting-only comparisons ride on it: a kerbal the timeline believes it created that the save does not carry, a kerbal it holds permanently gone that the save lists in a state a reservation cannot explain, and a tech node it claims to have researched that the save never unlocked. Purchased parts and strategies are reported as a plain census, because the reconstruction produces nothing to compare them against. Internal only.

- The rule that a flight's outcome may only be recorded through one place in the code is now enforced by the build instead of by reading. Deciding what became of a vessel has to go through a single entry point, because that decision is what retires the stale verdict about its crew - and the first pass at wiring every site to it was done by eye and missed two, one of them the exact path a re-flown craft takes when it is not the last leg of its flight. A check now walks the source and fails the build on any place that records an outcome directly, against a list of approved exceptions written line by line rather than file by file - a file-level list would have approved both of the misses, since each sat in a file whose neighbouring branch was already correct. Two further checks keep the list itself honest: one fails if an approved line no longer exists, the other if the walk stops finding anything to check. Internal only.
- The developer-only automated-test harness no longer destroys one run's evidence with the next. Each run's stored verdict, its copied game log, its screenshots and its summary page were all filed under a name stamped only to the minute, so two runs of the same scenario started inside the same minute were filed under the same name and the second silently wrote over the first - observed on two back-to-back runs 52 seconds apart, where a clean run's result and collected log were replaced by the later run's and nothing said so. A run now checks what is already filed and takes a fresh name rather than overwriting anything, reserves that name the moment it picks it so two runs started at the same instant cannot pick the same one, says in the log which name it moved to and why, and both runs then appear side by side on the results index. A run's own retry, which deliberately shares the run's name and is marked as attempt 2, is unaffected. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- When Parsek declines to hide a stock Tracking Station error, its log entry now says what it checked. The game rebuilds its Tracking Station vessel list whenever a vessel is destroyed, and that rebuild sometimes fails; Parsek reports such a failure rather than hiding it unless it can show one of its own ghost markers caused it. The report now also records whether a Parsek ghost teardown was actually running at that moment and how many ghosts existed. That paid for itself immediately: the one such error seen in testing had both readings at zero, which - with the timing and call stack from the same log - identified it as a stock problem that happens while the game is shutting down, nothing to do with Parsek. A second suppression rule was written for this and then withdrawn before release, because the same evidence showed it could have hidden exactly that stock error. No behaviour changed; the log says more. Internal only.
- One of the checks that decides whether Parsek may hide a stock Tracking Station error could never actually run. Before hiding one, Parsek asks the error report where inside the game's own method the failure came from, and refuses to hide it if the answer is somewhere Parsek has no business hiding. The game never reports that position for this method - Parsek's own patching of it is what removes it - and the check stopped reading at the first line rather than reading the rest of the report, so it could never reach an answer at all. For most of its life it counted for nothing while its own description said otherwise; the description was corrected shortly before this release, and this is the code catching up to it. The check now reads the whole report, treats a report carrying no position as no evidence either way rather than as a verdict, and writes its reading into the log line so the same gap cannot go unnoticed again. Against the current game that reading is still "no evidence" - confirmed on a live test flight that caught one of these errors and logged it - so nothing about when errors get hidden changes today; the check is simply honest about it now, and it works if a report ever does carry the position. Internal only.
- Settled an open tuning question about the developer-only automated Mun-orbit test flight instead of guessing at it. An operator watching a live run thought the stretch from entering the Mun's sphere of influence to the capture burn ran slower than it needed to, and named two settings to raise. The flight's own recorded numbers, plus a headless re-run of the decision logic against them, show both settings are inert on that stretch: one is a safety limit the healthy approach never gets within an hour of reaching, and the other governs a single decision poll. Effectively all of the approach is flown by the autopilot mod's own node executor - including a fixed ten-minute hold it performs before the capture burn it flies, which is the real cost and is not Parsek's to change. Nothing was changed, so no confirmation flight is owed; three new checks pin which actor flies which part, so a future change that makes either setting matter is caught. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only automated-test harness now records when an autopilot flight commits its mission from inside itself and then fails. The harness already refuses to run world-changing steps after a failed flight, but a mission can also commit mid-flight, before its own verdict exists, and that path was invisible - not dangerous in any run seen so far, since the missions that do it have only ever done so on their success path, and every run starts from a fresh copy of the save, but nothing said it had happened. Each run's result now records those mid-flight commands, counted and classified on the same scale as the harness's own steps. Deliberately reporting-only: no run's verdict changes, and the record is byte-identical for every run that has no such commands. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Re-checked, and marked up in the code itself, four known coordinate-frame mismatches in the predictor that extends an unfinished falling trajectory after a craft leaves the scene. All four are still present; each now carries a note naming the frame it uses, the likely correction, and the fact that they must be fixed together. Two can be shown wrong with no measurement at all - they build a single position-and-velocity pair out of two different coordinate systems - while the other two turn on an axis convention that has to be measured in the running game, so the entry now also spells out the one test flight that would settle all four. No behaviour changed. Internal only.
- Removed a dead branch from the recordings list's reveal path and gave the path real test coverage. The branch tried to switch off the archive filter to expose a recording it had already un-archived one line earlier, so it could never run; the surrounding code kept working only because un-archiving the recording is what reveals it. Nothing player-visible changes. Internal only.
- The developer-only automated-test harness can now read what a flight actually left in the save file, not just count recording files: a new pure-Python parser reads Parsek's own portion of the produced save (mission trees, per-recording end states, branch points, supersede rows, career tombstones, rewind points) and checks it against per-scenario structural expectations - how many timelines were superseded by a re-fly, whether a crew death left its tombstone, whether the rewind point survived. Until now the nightly rewind scenario declared exactly these assertions and they did nothing (recorded as "skipped, verifier pending"), so a merge that silently dropped one of two boards, or a re-fly that wrote no supersede row, could pass every check the harness had. The new checks run in report-only mode first - results are recorded with every run but move no verdict until each scenario's readings have been confirmed on a live run and the scenario explicitly opts in. The nightly rewind scenario has now done exactly that and is the first to have these checks switched on for real: its readings were confirmed on a live run, the checks were armed, and they were then deliberately made to fail once, to prove the check really does redden when the save does not match what the scenario expects. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only automated-test harness can now reach two places it never could: it can start the game directly in the Tracking Station, and it can leave the flight scene for the Space Center. Seven groups of Parsek's in-game self-tests were stranded because nothing in the harness could enter the Tracking Station at all, and a flight whose craft is destroyed could never have its mission committed unattended, because that commit only happens on leaving flight and no test command could leave. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The new leave-flight test command refuses, immediately and with a reason naming the exact prompt, in the cases where leaving flight would raise a merge confirmation that no automated driver can answer - instead of appearing to work and then silently hanging until the step runs out of time. The mis-spelled-scene case is refused the same way rather than quietly starting the game somewhere else, which would have let a test pass while checking nothing. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only automated-test harness can now switch vessels the way the game does. Until now it could only set the active vessel directly, which skips the code that handles a real "Switch To" click in the map view, so the tests meant to cover switching between craft mid-mission were never touching that code at all and would have kept passing if it broke. The new test command reproduces the click itself, and it refuses with a clear reason - rather than half-doing it - whenever a real click would have raised a merge prompt, whenever the target is out of physics range, and whenever the switch could not happen at all. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only automated-test command that ends a re-fly session now waits for the rewound mission to finish resuming before it triggers the exit, instead of racing it: issued too early, the exit slipped past the in-flight confirmation prompt and the session was concluded by the fallback prompt in the next scene, so the nightly test covering "rewind, then finish without flying again" never actually exercised the in-flight prompt or the fix that protects an idle re-fly attempt from being silently discarded. That test now requires the in-flight route end to end: the discard refusal, the in-flight prompt, and the immediate answer. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Fixed a developer-only automated-test command that drove a scene change without saving first, which no in-game route does: the re-fly session marker was therefore discarded before the merge dialog it was meant to answer even appeared, so the scenario covering "rewind, then finish without flying again" failed every night without producing a result. The same scenario also claimed two things it structurally could not test, and carried a stale exemption that could only have hidden an unrelated failure; both are corrected. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added the first developer-only automated test in which a kerbal actually dies: a crewed pod launches, deploys no parachute, and hits the ground, so that what Parsek records about a crew death can be checked by a real flight rather than only by unit tests. It judges the death by reading the kerbal's own roster status from the game instead of assuming a fatal-looking fall, and it has now been flown end to end. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Found while building that test (developer-facing, reported not fixed): when the craft you are recording is destroyed, the mission tree is set aside rather than committed, and it can only be committed later from outside the flight scene. The automated-test harness has no way to leave the flight scene, so an automated crash flight cannot commit its own mission, and nothing about the crash reaches the career timeline during that run. No player-facing effect - a player leaving the flight scene commits it normally. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change. (The harness limitation stated here was lifted later in this same release: it can now leave the flight scene for the Space Center, so an automated crash flight CAN commit its own mission - see "The developer-only automated-test harness can now reach two places it never could".)
- Added the first career save in the repo that carries a flyable craft, built headlessly from two existing test saves rather than by flying one. Every career-economy test until now had to be run from the space centre with nothing in flight. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Fixed a developer-only automated test that reported its flight successful while the kerbal it was supposed to save died: the mission's own checks all end when the craft reaches the exit window, minutes before the kerbal ever leaves the pod, so they could never see the outcome. The one check that did see it was recorded and then ignored by every gate. The harness now fails any run whose post-flight in-world steps report an error, and the mission result states in writing which part of the test it did not verify and which step owns it. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Diagnosed why the same test's kerbal died: its personal parachute cut itself seconds after opening because the kerbal was still touching the craft it had just left, and any bump above 3.5 m/s while a parachute is open makes the game cut it for good. The EVA step now waits until the kerbal is measurably clear of everything else before the parachute step runs, bounded both by a timer and by remaining altitude. Both this and the check above have now been flown end to end. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Five developer-only automated test flights were passing while blind to the thing they produce most of: each drops six boosters that Parsek records as their own debris recordings, and each flight's only numeric check accepted "one recording", so Parsek could have stopped recording dropped boosters entirely and all five would still have reported success. They now require the log line that records a booster becoming its own recording, and each flight's recording count starts at the number that flight actually measured (seven or eight, depending on whether it also drops a spent stage) instead of at one. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-test harness now rejects an unparseable log check when the scenario is written, and its preview command checks scenarios instead of only printing them. These checks are patterns, and one written the natural way (pasting in a log line containing parentheses) was unusable until a run finished; on the longest scenario that mistake cost 47 minutes of flying to discover. This catches the unparseable form, not a pattern that parses but never matches. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Most of Parsek's in-game self-tests only ran when a developer triggered them by hand. Added 14 developer-only scenarios so 14 more categories of them run unattended; all 14 have been run end to end, pass, and now check an exact test count measured from a real run. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The full inventory of in-game test categories is now derived from the source rather than listed by hand, with each category marked as wired, wireable-but-blocked (and by what), or genuinely not runnable unattended (and why). Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- 68 of Parsek's in-game self-tests could only ever be run by a developer clicking a button, because the unattended runner never called the one entry point that knows how to reload a clean flight between destructive tests. It can now, so those 68 become automatable, and a first scenario drives two of them (a real recording taken through a real launch and a real exit to the Space Center, both branches of the merge prompt). Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Closed another way an automated test scenario could report success while checking nothing: a test that inspects stored recordings passes trivially when there are none. The scenarios affected now load the full synthetic recording set and verify it arrived. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Fixed a developer test-harness bug that made any test category with a hyphen in its name impossible to pin a test count for, even though the game reported those counts correctly. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-test flight autopilot can now issue any developer test-command mid-flight, not just "commit the mission tree", and a new test flight uses that to fly a full rewind LOOP: fly, commit, rewind, then fly again and check the re-flown attempt was recorded. It judges the rewind by watching the game clock actually run backward rather than by trusting the command's own success report, and it stops the recorder and confirms it is actually idle before rewinding: committing a mission tree leaves the craft flying and immediately starts a new recording on it, which the rewind command legitimately refuses to run over. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Known issue found and diagnosed by that new test flight (developer-facing, reported not yet fixed): when you rewind and fly the attempt again, the new flight is recorded into a brand-new mission tree instead of into the re-flown attempt's own recording. Because that recording stays empty, the merge declines to mark the old branch as replaced, so you end up with the original branch and the re-flown branch both live as two unrelated histories, and the re-fly's core promise ("this attempt replaces that one") silently does not happen. On developer builds it additionally leaves the merge half-finished and reports an error every time the save is loaded. No recordings are lost. (That second half was fixed later in this same release - see Fixes, "Concluding a Re-Fly that never flew ... no longer leaves the save stuck part-way through the merge and failing on every later load" - and an attempt that ends up with nothing recording into it now says so on screen and in the log at the moment it happens. The primary issue above, the new flight landing in a brand-new tree, remains open and reported.)
- Two rewind test scenarios that were marked "operator only, cannot run unattended" are now on the nightly rotation: the reason given (no way to enter the flight scene) was never true, and the other blocker they cited has since shipped. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added two developer-only automated-test scenarios that check PLAYBACK rather than recording: they drive the in-game map-render parity tests, which compare the orbit geometry Parsek actually draws for a ghost against the geometry it recorded, and fail if that comparison never actually ran instead of passing on an empty measurement. Both have now been run end to end. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-test harness no longer reports a render anomaly when a test's own diagnostic message merely mentions one by name: it now looks for an actual anomaly report rather than the word appearing anywhere in the log. One scenario was failing on a clean run because of it. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- A developer-only test scenario that switches a diagnostic tracer on no longer leaves it switched on for every later test run on that install: the harness now resets the shared Parsek settings file to a known state before and after each run, so long unattended flights stop paying for a tracer they never asked for. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Fixed a developer test scenario that reported success while running no tests at all: its in-game test batch loaded a save with no vessels, so every test in the batch was skipped for needing the flight scene, and the scenario's only check ("no failures") could not tell that apart from every test passing. All batch-running scenarios now state exactly how many tests must run and pass, and the harness refuses any scenario whose check an empty batch could satisfy, or that runs a second test batch nothing would check. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Those stated test counts are now checked against the in-game tests themselves, so adding an in-game test fails immediately in the developer test suite, naming the scenario and the new count, instead of silently breaking an automated scenario on the next unattended overnight run. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added two developer-only automated-test scenarios that run the existing in-game mission-loop and re-aim/periodicity test categories against the live game's real planet data. These tests existed but had never run unattended because no scenario referenced them. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change. On its first run the mission-loop scenario immediately caught a leak (below).
- Fixed developer in-game tests leaving stray recording files behind: a test that registers a synthetic mission tree through the real commit path writes that tree's trajectory files to the save, and the test's own cleanup only removed the tree from memory, so the files stayed on disk forever. Every such test now deletes the files it created - including the ones that reach the commit through the merge dialog rather than calling it directly - and the shared cleanup refuses to touch any recording the game still knows about. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added two developer-only automated test flights to Eve: a flyby (now flying green) and an orbit that captures, parks and closes the mission tree there. They are the first tests to fly INWARD toward the sun rather than outward, which needed three fixes to the test autopilot: it now rounds out its parking orbit before the interplanetary burn (the autopilot mod mis-sizes that burn from an out-of-round park), only plans course corrections (and only crawls its time-warp toward them) once actually on the interplanetary leg, and reports at plan time whether a planned transfer reaches the target's orbit at all. The Eve orbit flight stays operator-run until its first green result rather than joining the nightly rotation. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added two developer-only automated test flights that land on the Mun and on Minmus and close the mission tree while sitting on the surface, so recordings that END on another world are now covered end to end (every existing flight either ends in orbit around another world or lands back on Kerbin). The landing watchdog that gives up on a stalled descent no longer fires on a single frame, and stands down entirely in the last stretch above the ground where its altitude-drop test cannot be met; the descent time budget bounds that stretch instead. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The commit log line that names where each recording ended now reports the right world for a landed or splashed recording. It used to print the last world the craft ORBITED, so a flight that circled the Mun and then came home and landed read as ending at the Mun. Log wording only; no gameplay change.
- When an automated test flight fails to reach the state it was flying toward, the harness now runs only the teardown that closes the recording and quits the game, instead of carrying on with the rest of the scripted steps (on one failed run that meant sending a kerbal out the hatch while the craft was still falling at terminal velocity). Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- An automated test flight that gives up because its time warp is running without actually advancing time now cancels that warp before the harness closes the recording and quits, so the shutdown steps no longer run against a still-warping game. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Career recalculation is slightly cheaper: the walk now skips a redundant re-sort of the action list when nothing changed it. Recalculated career values are unchanged.
- Added a developer-only way to run in-game test batches unattended, driven entirely by launch-time environment variables, plus a new set of recording-integrity checks that run in-game. It is completely inert in a normal game and never changes anything Parsek saves.
- The developer-only test-command channel's game-load step now detects a failed load (a save that returns to the menu, or one that never finishes loading) and reports it as an error instead of waiting indefinitely. Inert in a normal game; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only test-command channel's time-jump step now reports success correctly instead of always timing out (the clock keeps ticking past the target while the jump settles, which the old check mistook for a miss), and rejects a nonsensical jump target up front. Inert in a normal game; no gameplay change.
- Added three developer-only automated-test scenarios covering the live recording start/stop, commit, and discard cycle plus an in-game recording-integrity sweep over the synthetic corpus. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added a developer-only automated-test fixture that injects a rewindable recording tree (a crashed booster with a rewind point) plus the first two rewind-and-merge test scenarios that drive it. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added the first developer-only automated-test scenarios that drive a single career action (research a node, upgrade a facility, hire or dismiss a kerbal) and check the career totals moved by exactly the expected amount, across Career, Science, and Sandbox modes. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added the three career/science/sandbox save fixtures those career-action scenarios load, with pinned starting funds, science, and reputation and a fixed roster. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only test-command discard step now also removes the discarded recording's leftover data files from disk, which the first full automated run caught being stranded permanently. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-test provisioner now writes a complete kRPC server configuration instead of a partial one; the partial file silently disabled all remote-control command processing, which blocked the first autopilot-flown test flight. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added the two stock-craft fixture saves (Jumping Flea pad hop, Kerbal X orbiter) the autopilot-flown test scenarios launch from, and the automated-test game instance now runs fully muted. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- A destroyed test-flight craft now ends its automated mission within seconds instead of holding the game open for the full time budget, and the failure names the real cause. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The autopilot-flown orbital test scenario now completes end to end: launched, flown to orbit by autopilot, recorded, and verified green - including the dropped boosters being recorded as debris. Required a MechJeb integration re-pin plus mission-logic fixes found across five live flights. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Fixed the developer-only test-command channel's LoadGame verb, which always failed when booting a flight save straight from the main menu: it now adopts the loaded game before the flight scene change so the stock loader has a current game to read. Inert in a normal game; no gameplay change.
- The automation-stack provisioner now installs the full Parsek payload (version file plus toolbar icons), not just the plugin, so a provisioned instance no longer floods its log with a missing-icon error every frame.
- The in-game test runner's post-batch restore no longer times out on a vessel with no staging (a bare command pod): the stage-manager wait now recognizes that such a vessel legitimately has zero stages. Staged vessels wait exactly as before.
- Added two developer-only automated test flights that fly to the Mun and to Minmus, burn into a stable orbit there, hold it, and finish the mission recording while still parked around that moon, the first automated check of a recording that ends and is saved in another body's sphere of influence. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automation-stack provisioner no longer reports a provisioned instance as drifted after every game launch: runtime caches mods write under their PluginData folders are excluded from the drift check, and a re-copy now clears stale leftovers first. Developer-only tooling; no gameplay change.
- The offline recording analyzer can now record a per-save baseline of already-known, accepted findings, so a gated run over a save with permanent already-filed issues fails only on genuinely new findings. The baseline never hides a finding from the report and never applies to a fresh mission save.
- Implemented the developer-only automation-stack provisioner's live phases: it clones a pinned KSP instance, builds the kRPC TestingTools shim from source, installs the pinned kRPC / KRPC.MechJeb / Parsek stack, and verifies (and can self-repair) the instance against a manifest. It never writes to your KSP install and never changes anything Parsek saves.
- Route resource transfers now log a per-resource cargo delta line (LiquidFuel, MonoPropellant, and so on) when a docked route window closes at undock, naming exactly how much each side gained or lost across the docked period. Log-only; no gameplay change.
- Added the developer-only two-vessel dock/transfer/undock automated-test lane and a headless fixture-forge that stamps its pre-placed-station save without an operator flight; each vehicle now separates its spent lifter stage and ignites its orbital engine after circularizing so it docks as its orbital stage only, never a full stack. Test-tooling only; not yet flown; no gameplay change.
- The automation-stack provisioner now stamps the kRPC server settings so a provisioned instance starts and accepts connections without a manual in-game click, and treats a later change to those settings as instance drift. Developer-only tooling; no gameplay change.
- The automation-stack provisioner now skips the copy, build, and extract work for anything already installed identically when re-provisioning a clean instance, and its drift check now catches a stray file added inside a stack component's folder (kRPC caches under PluginData are still ignored, since the game rewrites them). Developer-only tooling; no gameplay change.
- Added the developer-only automated-testing harness that runs in-game test scenarios start to finish with no human in the loop and classifies each run (pass, real failure, environment-invalid, or killed-on-timeout), with a coverage ledger tracking what got tested. It never touches a normal game install and changes nothing Parsek saves.
- The offline recording analyzer now distinguishes a still-rewindable recording whose rewind save is missing (a real defect, flagged as a failure) from a sealed recording's missing rewind save (a benign dangling reference, still only a warning). Developer-only tooling; no gameplay change.
- Added the developer-only mission library: the automated-testing harness can now FLY missions (a pad hop, a MechJeb ascent to orbit) through kRPC while Parsek records them, judging the flight by tolerance windows so autopilot variance never masquerades as a Parsek defect. Live flights pending an operator session; everything else is headless-tested.
- The developer-only test-command channel gained four new verbs: invoke a rewind, answer the post-re-fly merge dialog, jump time forward, and perform KSC career actions (research, facility upgrade, hire, dismiss) through the real stock paths - unlocking automated rewind and career-economy test scenarios. Inert in a normal game; no gameplay change.
- Added the developer-only ledger oracle: the harness now cross-checks career money, science, and reputation against two independent witnesses (what stock KSP granted at event time, and what the save file says afterwards), with Parsek's own arithmetic deliberately excluded from both, so any amount the ledger invents or loses is caught as a drift. Live verification pending an operator session; everything else is headless-tested.
- The automated-testing harness now re-runs only a flaked verifier tool (a wedged analyzer or a transient log check) against the same run instead of re-flying the whole ~10-minute scenario, and correctly reads a multi-category in-game test batch's combined pass/fail summary. Developer-only tooling; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only test-command channel now lets research-node run in Science mode (where R&D is live) in addition to Career, and gained a SaveGame verb that persists the current game in-place so a test can save and reload within one launch. Inert in a normal game; no gameplay change.
- Added an in-game test category and an unattended automated-test scenario covering this release's route-and-rewind behaviors (pause/resume timeline rows, dormant routes across a rewind, restored route status and counters, discarded post-rewind science) so they are verified automatically instead of by manual playtest. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Fixed the pad-hop automated test flight never actually opening its parachute: it now arms the chute at the apoapsis crossing while the craft is still slow, because stock refuses to open one at terminal velocity in dense air. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The pad-hop test flight's success terminal now requires the parachute to be observed open rather than merely commanded, so a terminal-velocity impact can no longer pass as a chute landing. It still also requires the craft to have reached the ground, and a missed deployment window now fails fast with a named reason instead of running out the clock. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added a new autopilot-flown automated test scenario, proven live: ascend to orbit, deorbit, reenter, and splash down intact, with the full flight (dropped boosters and the deorbited stage included) recorded and verified green. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added a Mun flyby / free-return autopilot-flown test scenario: ascend to orbit, plan and execute a transfer to the Mun, fly through its sphere of influence, and return into Kerbin's, covering cross-SOI recording under time warp. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added a Minmus flyby test scenario reusing the same flight machinery with Minmus-sized parameters. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Added a Duna interplanetary flyby test scenario: eject from a high Kerbin park at the next transfer window, coast through the Sun's sphere of influence with time-triggered course corrections, fly past Duna, and exit into solar orbit. Flown and passing unattended (546 km flyby, free return). Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only test-command channel gained three EVA verbs - send a kerbal out an airlock, plant a flag, and board a craft - driving the same stock paths a player's hatch/plant/board clicks use, plus three automated scenarios covering ground EVA with a flag plant, an orbital EVA re-board, and a sequential multi-kerbal EVA; all three have now flown green and exercise Parsek's crew-EVA branch, flag-event, and board-merge recording. Inert in a normal game; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only test-command channel's hire-kerbal action no longer charges the recruit cost twice: it was manually mirroring a funds debit that stock already applies automatically when a kerbal is hired, so the funds pool dropped by double the hire cost. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The developer-only test-command channel gained an EVA-parachute verb that arms a kerbal's personal chute through the same stock call a player's key press makes, waits for the canopy to actually open, and can hold until the kerbal lands or splashes down alive, plus an automated scenario that hops a craft, chutes it, sends the kerbal out mid-air, and lands them under their own parachute. This exercises Parsek's mid-flight EVA branch, the kerbal's own atmospheric recording, and the two-phase chute events recorded on the kerbal. Inert in a normal game; no gameplay change.
- That mid-air EVA test scenario now opens the test craft's parachute just after the top of its hop instead of on the way down, and waits for the game to report an actual open canopy before sending the kerbal out. Deploying near the ground was ineffective: the craft was already at terminal velocity, where the game refuses to open a parachute at all, so the run could never reach the EVA. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The mid-air EVA test now requires two consecutive readings to agree that the craft is safely under canopy before it sends the kerbal out, and the EVA-parachute verb no longer reports success on the poll it first reads the kerbal as gone. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The automated-test harness's check that no unexpected career reward fired during a test run had never actually looked at anything: the log patterns it searched for were written from the design document rather than from a real game log, and matched a shape the game does not print, so the check silently passed on every run ever made. The patterns are rewritten from award lines measured in real flights, and they now also carry the reward's own reason (the game names it, e.g. a speed record or a lost vessel), which is what tells two same-sized rewards in the same instant apart. A reward the scenario itself declared is now recognised as its own (matched by when it happened, which pool it moved and by how much, optionally pinned to the reward's reason name), so only genuinely undeclared rewards are reported. Because this makes a dormant check live for the first time, unexpected rewards are REPORTED rather than failed by default, with a per-scenario switch to start failing on them once a run has shown what a healthy flight's rewards actually are. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The harness's render-anomaly check listed one anomaly name that nothing in Parsek can ever report, so it advertised coverage of exactly the class of glitch the map-rendering work has been chasing while being structurally unable to see it. That dead name is retired from the checked set (and kept on a named retired list, so it reds if a reporter for it ever appears), and each checked anomaly can now be given an allowed count instead of only being allowed or not, so a rare harmless blip staying rare is a different claim from it becoming a per-frame storm. No scenario sets a count yet; the per-run counts are now recorded so one can be chosen from real data. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Nothing in the harness had ever read a log line Parsek did not write, so a run full of raw game crashes (null-reference errors, an interface-layout error storm) passed every check the harness has. Each run now counts those and records the numbers in its result, without failing anything, plus an opt-in per-scenario ceiling that no scenario sets yet. The counts are recorded on killed runs too, since a crash storm is a prime suspect for whatever hung the game. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The reward-check rewrite above was itself half wrong, and is now corrected: the funds reward line it had been taught to look for was copied by analogy from the reputation one rather than measured, and the game turns out never to print a funds or science reward at all - only reputation. The funds pattern is retired to a named list, so anyone re-adding one has to make that decision deliberately, and the search for a science line is called off rather than left as an open task. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Extended the developer tests for what happens when a recording saved by an older, incompatible version of Parsek's storage format is found in a save. The load-time drop and the basic reference cleanup were already covered; what is new is the full on-disk round trip (write a real save and its data files, reload, save again, and confirm the second reload is identical), the check that the dropped recording's now-unreferenced data files are moved to a quarantine folder rather than deleted, three more tree shapes (dropping a leaf, dropping a recording with several children, dropping the recording the save was actively recording into), and direct tests of the per-recording reference-clearing step. Test-only; no gameplay change.
- The harness's unexpected-career-reward check can now be armed on a scenario that actually flies. It matched a declared reward by the exact instant it happened, and a real flight cannot promise that instant: the same crash landed at three slightly different times across three runs of the same craft, so on the first scenario ever to capture real reward lines every one of them - all correctly declared - was reported as unexpected. A scenario can now declare the time WINDOW a reward should land in ("the impact happens between 100 and 140 seconds") instead of the exact moment; everything else about the check (amounts, which pool moved, the reward's reason name, one declared reward explaining at most one captured one) is unchanged, and a reward with no readable time never matches a window. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The harness's pre-launch check on a scenario's declared career rewards now runs the full post-flight validator instead of a hand-written subset of it, so every kind of typo in a declared reward is caught before the game boots rather than after the flight, where the cost is a whole test run instead of a second. This started as two specific gaps (a reward timestamp that is not a real number, and a reward entry that is not a table) and grew when review showed the line drawn between the two checks was arbitrary: a mistyped ordinal or reward-reason name was still costing a flight. One rule is deliberately left to the post-flight check, because it can only be judged once the game's log exists. A sweep runs both checks against each other over every malformed shape so they cannot drift apart again. Separately, an implausibly large number in a declared timestamp used to crash the whole batch of scenarios instead of rejecting just the one bad scenario; it now rejects cleanly. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The unexpected-reward check is now enforcing for the first time, on the crew-loss scenario. It had been written as a hard failure but had never once run against real captured rewards, so it stayed advisory everywhere. The reward capture only ever sees reputation, and of the scenarios that earn any, the crew-loss ledger flight is the one that can carry the declarations the check needs - which makes it the only place the check has anything to look at. It was armed the careful way: one flight to record what rewards the flight really produces, a second to confirm the newly declared time windows match all of them, and a third with the check switched on and failing for real. All three passed first time. The windows are the mission's phases rather than exact instants, which those same three flights justified - one reward moved between runs on the same afternoon. Review caught that the first draft of those windows was measured against the wrong clock (they bound absolute game time, which also counts however long the harness spends on the launchpad before ignition, not just the flight), so they were widened to clear that before merging. A missing reward is still caught by the separate save comparison, and the run now also requires the game's own reward lines to appear at all, so a reward check with nothing to check can no longer read as a pass. Every other scenario is unaffected and still advisory. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- A harness run that asks for pre-made recordings to be injected into its save now checks, before launching the game, that the injection actually wrote them. The injection tool could report success having written nothing (its deliberate no-rebuild mode runs zero tests in a freshly set up workspace, and its log-in-use probe declines through the same success path), so the run booted the game anyway and failed minutes later with an error naming the wrong component - which has cost three full test flights, one of them twice over on the same day. The miss now stops the run in seconds, before the game ever boots, with a message naming the actual cause and the one-line remedy, and it is not retried (the same workspace would miss the same way). Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- The source-scan that keeps the harness's pinned in-game test counts honest no longer quietly assumes a test it cannot read is batch-enabled: an in-game test whose batch-participation flag is written as anything but a literal true or false is now counted as NOT batch-runnable and flagged loudly by the same sweep that already catches an unreadable category or scene, instead of silently loosening the pinned counts in the forgiving direction. Every test in the tree today uses a literal, so nothing changes until someone writes one that does not. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.
- Two developers (or two agents) working in parallel checkouts can no longer corrupt each other's automated test runs. The harness and the setup tool each kept their own separate lock file and never read the other's, so the routine "re-deploy the mod into the test game" step could overwrite the game's files underneath a run that was already in progress but between game launches - producing a flight that runs the wrong build and fails in a way that looks exactly like a real Parsek bug. They now share one lock covering the whole machine, which is the right scope: the automated tests drive the game through a fixed network port and a single graphics card, so two runs can never safely overlap regardless of which game folder each one targets. The harness also holds that lock for its entire run instead of releasing and re-taking it between scenarios, closing a window where a second run could seize the game mid-way through an overnight batch and kill every remaining scenario. Both tools claim the lock through one shared routine, so two runs starting at the same instant cannot both believe they won, and a run that finds an abandoned lock verifies what it is taking over before removing it — an earlier draft of this fix had each tool doing its own claiming, and two reviews showed both of its versions could still let a second run through. If a run does lose its lock part-way, it now stops rather than carrying on unprotected. A lock left behind by a run that was force-killed is still cleaned up automatically, and now also expires on a timer, so a stale lock can no longer block the machine indefinitely if the operating system happens to reuse the dead run's process number. A refused run names which checkout, which run, and since when the lock has been held, plus the file to delete if it is certain nothing is running. Test-tooling only; no gameplay change.

## 0.10.3

### Features

- The first time Parsek opens one of your existing saves, it now makes a one-time safety backup of that save, taken before Parsek changes anything, as a separate timestamped "pre-Parsek" entry in the Load menu, so you can always return to your career as it was before installing Parsek. It runs once per save, includes your saved craft, skips brand-new empty careers, and can be turned off under Settings > Data Management. Note: it can only protect saves whose first Parsek use happens after this version, and resuming a backup with Parsek installed lets Parsek manage it again.
- Re-aimed looped landings now connect their arrival to the re-aimed transfer: the recorded approach, capture, and destination parking turn rigidly about the destination so the incoming line meets them, while the descent and touchdown stay exactly at the recorded landing site. Any mission shape outside the supported single-destination landing profile renders exactly as before.
- Supply runs that transfer across the claw (Advanced Grabbing Unit) can now become Supply Routes, with the same proof rigor as docked runs: a claw grab opens the same connection window as a dock, transfers across it deliver or pick up normally, and asteroid grabs count as structural (mining gains stay covered by harvest provenance). Unrecognized modded coupling types are rejected by name instead of being treated as docks, and grappled connections are labeled in the route panels.
- A mission docked by a vessel from another mission can now loop its whole shared journey from its own side: the Missions window offers a "Partner journey" row for each such dock, and including it pulls the docked stretch and the vessel's post-undock flight (recorded in the other mission's tree) into this mission's selection and loop. Cross-tree missions loop at their faithful recorded cadence (no launch-window phase lock yet); existing missions and saves are unchanged.
- A looped multi-moon tour (the "Jool-5" profile) now aligns its moon encounters on replay instead of rendering every encounter seam disconnected: with 2+ SOI-entered moons at the destination, the per-loop arrival hold aligns the moons' JOINT CONFIGURATION - the hold period is the configuration's recurrence (for the stock resonant Laythe/Vall/Tylo, ~one Tylo orbit), found with the same near-coincidence scheduling the launch side already uses, and every moon (plus any tidally locked moon landing, whose rotation collapses into its orbital phase) lands within its SOI tolerance. The alignment is honest about its finite horizon: the resonance drifts a few seconds per recurrence, so the engage log reports how many consecutive synodic windows stay in tolerance (~40 for the stock inner three) before the configuration drifts out. A configuration that does not recur (Bop/Pol legs, a non-tidally-locked moon landing, a landing on the gas giant itself, or too little loop slack) fails closed to faithful with an amber reason naming the shape, periods, and residuals - the previous silent Jool-class decline is gone. Station-bearing multi-moon shapes stay fail-closed with amber. Design: `docs/dev/design-mission-multimoon-alignment.md` (M-MIS-6); moon-to-moon leg re-aim inside the destination system remains deferred (M-MIS-7), gated on this feature's playtest.
- A looped interplanetary mission that both LANDS and docks with a station at the same destination now aligns BOTH on replay (the D8 landing+station dual, previously fail-closed with an amber "no single arrival hold aligns both periods"): the arrival hold snaps each loop onto the station's orbital phase exactly and extends by whole station orbits (bounded, at most 64) until the landing rotation phase is also within its alignment tolerance, re-solved per loop so neither alignment ever drifts. The launch cadence stays synodic (every transfer window is still a launch window). Geometry that cannot jointly align within tolerance and budget (for example under Precise landing-body alignment, or incommensurate station/rotation periods) keeps the fail-closed amber, now naming the measured tolerance miss. With landing-body alignment Off (the rotation A/B's "Off (frequent)"), the shape degrades to the plain station hold instead of failing closed - the previously deferred mode-aware D8 resolution. This wires the until-now unwired `DestinationArrivalSolver.SolveArrivalWindow` (the M-MIS-4 post-M4c follow-up); station+moon, moon-orbiting-station, and Jool-class station shapes stay fail-closed with updated amber reasons naming what is still unsupported.
- Supply routes now draw their path on the map: each committed route shows its recorded launch-to-dock route as a line on the flight map and in the Tracking Station, so you can see where a route runs instead of only reading its panel. A new "Show supply route paths on map" setting (on by default) toggles them, and the lines use the same style as ghost trajectory lines. Inter-body routes draw their recorded paths at both ends — the launch/ascent at the origin body and the approach at the destination body — while the transfer between them stays with the route ghost's own render, since the transfer geometry changes with every launch window.
- A supply route's detail panel now lists its recent cycles' cargo flow (newest first, last 5): what each cycle charged or took from where, picked up where, and delivered where, with shortfall cycles highlighted, so a route that is bleeding cargo (for example a crashed run that still debits its depot) is visible at a glance.
- Docked stretches are now selectable mission intervals: a dock (or a kerbal boarding) splits the vessel's timeline in the Missions window, the docked interval shows the combined vessel's real controller and crew counts (no more undercounting the station you docked to), and unchecking the pre-dock interval starts the mission's render at the dock. Existing saves keep their exact selections; old exclusions automatically cover the new docked sub-intervals they always covered.
- Supply routes now deliver at the displayed dispatch interval: the docked loading stretch no longer pads the realized cycle, so a route whose interval was shorter than the old launch-to-undock window delivers more often than before, and the route ghost retires at the dock instead of sitting docked until the undock.
- Supply run candidates can now be dismissed: each candidate and near-miss row in the Logistics window gets a Dismiss button that hides trees you never intend to run as routes, and a collapsed "Dismissed (N)" list at the bottom of the Candidates section lets you restore any of them later.
- Undock-to-undock depot shuttles can now become supply routes: a run that starts mid-flight but begins its cargo run at a recorded docked-origin window (dock at depot A, load, undock, deliver at depot B) is accepted instead of rejected, with depot A as the route's origin. The route renders and loops only the transit leg - from the origin undock to the delivery dock - so the pre-run flight and the docked loading stay are not replayed, and the dispatch interval matches the transit time. Launch-rooted routes are unchanged; shuttle shapes that still cannot be routed (an unrecorded origin dock, or overlapping docked stretches) keep their specific rejection reason naming the recorded docked-origin moment instead of the generic "starts undocked with cargo already aboard" message.
- A supply route held because another route reserved a shared depot's cargo for its own in-flight cycle now says so in the Logistics window, naming the reserving route, instead of wrongly claiming the depot is out of that resource.
- A held supply route now names its specific blocker directly in its Status cell (for example "Held: Depot A out of Ore" or "Held: waiting for 'Return Run'") instead of a generic status sentence with the reason hidden in the tooltip. Long reasons are shortened in the cell; the full text stays in the tooltip and the detail panel.
- Committing a flight that qualifies as a Supply Route now prompts you once: a screen message announces it and the Parsek window shows a small banner with Open Logistics / Dismiss buttons (Dismiss also hides the candidate, reversible from the Dismissed list). Each flight prompts at most once, and never during test runs.
- Supply routes now work between planets: delivery follows the transfer windows the ghost flies, and the cadence setting delivers every Nth window.
- A supply route that was dispatched and then rewound past no longer leaves the depot charged with the cargo undelivered: the abandoned-future route ledger entries are now dropped at the rewind so the re-flown route re-delivers exactly once and is charged exactly once.

### Fixes

- A recording's vessel or EVA kerbal no longer materializes overlapping another craft when the primary spawn path is rejected and the degraded fallback runs: the collision-avoidance walkback position is now preserved through the fallback, and a landed endpoint recorded with exactly zero velocity no longer flakily rejects the primary spawn.
- A re-aimed looped landing's arrival approach no longer rotates the wrong way around the destination body: the arrival re-stitch read its rotation angle with an inverted sign on live KSP, doubling the gap at the SOI-entry seam instead of closing it. The touchdown site was never affected; caught by the in-game landing-coincidence canary on the first full test sweep.
- The Settings "Defaults" button now also restores "Show supply route paths on map" to on; previously that single toggle was left unchanged while every other setting reset to its default.
- A recorded vessel or EVA kerbal that re-materializes above the surface without a stored terminal orbit (breakup debris, an in-flight EVA, or a vessel left docked or coasting) no longer appears off-position and flips its situation a frame later. Its orbit was rebuilt by feeding an absolute world position and an unconverted velocity to KSP's state-vector API, which reads them in the wrong reference frame and produces an out-of-band orbit; the rebuild now converts them to the body-relative frame the API expects.
- A campaign save whose committed trees and missions failed to load (leaving the in-memory store empty while the recording sidecars still exist on disk) is no longer hollowed out by the next save: Parsek now detects that load fault and re-writes the trees and missions from the on-disk save instead of overwriting it with an empty set, so a one-time load failure can no longer progressively erase a save's committed recordings.
- Map ghost icons no longer snap visibly along their orbit at extreme time-warp (roughly 344x and up): the map-orbit refresh ran on a fixed half-second real-time timer, which at those rates spans hundreds of game-seconds per tick, letting the icon ride a stale orbit and jump ~1 Mm on each refresh. The refresh cadence now scales with the warp rate so one tick never covers more than 30 game-seconds; behavior at normal speed is unchanged.
- Rotated burn-leg trajectory lines on the map (the "bridge" arcs connecting two orbits, e.g. an escape burn after a phasing loiter) no longer slowly change shape while time passes at warp: the leg's points were re-read at the live planet rotation every frame and re-rotated onto the fixed orbit seam, visibly reshaping the arc's interior at exactly the planet's spin rate. Anchored legs are now drawn frozen in the non-rotating frame (each point where it actually was at its recorded time), so the bridge shape is rigid; launch ascents, descents, and other surface-glued legs keep rotating with the planet as before.
- A looped re-aim arrival now hands off cleanly in flight too: while the descent clip plays, the transfer/loiter member's flight 3D ghost hides (mirroring the tracking-station icon handoff), so only the descending vessel exists at the handoff instead of a second ghost still circling the parking orbit. The map/TS icon handoff and the flight ghost handoff now share one decision, so the two scenes can never disagree on when the handoff fires.
- The route detail panel's recent-cycles lines now surface stored-part inventory shortfalls: a cycle short only on inventory items gets the shortfall highlight and a "(source was short)" note, and a fully blocked inventory pickup reads "picked up 0 of N inventory item(s)" instead of "picked up nothing" with no explanation.

### Internals & Tests

- Fixed two FLIGHT in-game tests (`EvaSpawnWalkbackOnOverlap`, `ExplosionAnchorPosition_BelowTerrain_ClampsBeforeWatchHold`) failing whenever the test batch ran from an orbiting station rather than a landed vessel: the EVA walkback fixture now sizes itself from the active vessel and skips loudly when that vessel cannot host a walkback, and the loop explosion anchor now scales its tolerance with the scene's float grid instead of a fixed 1 mm epsilon. Test fixtures only; production behavior is unchanged.
- The in-game test runner (Ctrl+Shift+T) now has a search box that filters the category/test list live as you type, matching category and test names case-insensitively (with an "x" to clear). The filter only changes what is shown, so Run All and the per-category Run buttons still run every test regardless of what is typed.
- Fixed the undock-to-undock shuttle in-game gate (`LogisticsShuttleRuntimeTests`) failing its first live run: the synthetic tree's recordings never carried their tree id, so the built route could not derive its backing mission and the loop-unit resolve returned nothing. Test fixture only; production route behavior is unchanged.
- Added an isolated-tier in-game canary (`MapRenderHighWarpCanaryInGameTest`, MapRender category) that automates the high-warp map-render validation recipe: with map-render tracing forced on and a real looped station/reaim ghost live on the map, it steps TimeWarp 50x to 1000x and back and asserts the probe fires zero icon-jump anomalies and any anchored bridge leg drew in the inertial basis.
